Early scholars note that the first two are events and the third is a condition. They note too that the passage spends most of its words on it. The closing comment repeats a line used earlier in the surah, about the signs being turned in different directions, so that they might grasp them.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the audience was a city held together by a fragile balance of clans. Mecca had no ruler and no standing force; it worked because rival families found it profitable to cooperate around a sanctuary. Everyone listening had heard of towns and tribes destroyed from within by feud. The third possibility named here was the one they had actually seen.

keyTerms.note: Groups formed around a following, from a root meaning to spread or to follow. The plural describes a body that has separated into camps, each with its own allegiance, rather than a simple disagreement.
From the root for clothing, so the sense is of things becoming entangled and hard to tell apart. Applied to a community, it names the state where nobody can say clearly what the quarrel is.

The causative of tasting, used through the Quran for consequence experienced first hand. Here what is tasted is supplied by other people, which makes the affliction one a community administers to itself.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian feuds ran for generations. A killing in one season brought an answering killing in the next. The tally could run on past the point where anyone recalled the first wrong. The long war between two tribes near Medina had worn out both sides within living memory. Listeners did not have to imagine a community tasting its own violence. They could name the families.
studies.didYouKnow: The comment that closes this ayah, about turning the signs in different directions, appears twice in this surah within twenty ayat. One time it ends with a note that they still turn away. Here it ends in the hope that they will understand. The same clause is given two different endings, which is itself an example of what it describes.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Division inside a group is listed beside disasters from the sky and from the ground, as something of the same order. That raises the stakes on how a community treats itself. The passage does not make factions a lesser problem, handled by people while the real events come from elsewhere. It also leaves the whole list in the conditional. What is being described is capacity. The point of describing it is understanding, not fear.

crossReferences.why: Gives the counterpart instruction: hold to God's rope together and do not scatter into separate parties.
Names the same fracturing, of those who split their religion and each faction rejoicing in its own.
Warns that quarrelling among themselves is what drains a community's strength away.

studies.applyIt: Think of a group you belong to that is quietly splitting. A family, a workplace, a neighbourhood. Find the one conversation nobody is having, because everyone assumes someone else should start it. You do not have to solve anything. Ask one person in the other camp what they really think. Then listen to the whole answer.
studies.explainEasier: God is able to send trouble on people from above them or from under their feet. He can also split them into groups and let them hurt each other. He explains this so people will understand.

studies.title: I Am Not Your Keeper
studies.meaning: The rejection is stated plainly and so is the fact it does not alter: your people denied it, and it is the truth. Then the burden is set down. He is not a keeper over them, which early scholars explain as a release from responsibility for outcomes rather than from the work of delivering the message. The second ayah adds the only thing left to say about timing. Every piece of news has a settled place where it comes to rest, and you will know it then.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, after a run of ayat describing what God is able to do and what the listeners keep refusing. This is where the surah turns and speaks to the one carrying the message rather than to those declining it. The classical sources do not report an occasion. The phrase about his own people has weight in a city where the objectors were relatives and neighbours.

keyTerms.note: The agent who manages another's affairs and answers for them. Denying the role removes both the authority to compel and the liability for the result, which are two halves of one office.
News that carries consequence, the same word used earlier in this surah for what will reach those who mocked. Its reappearance ties this promise back to that one.
A noun of place and time from the verb to settle. It can name where something comes to rest or when, and the ambiguity lets the phrase cover both without choosing between them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A trusted agent was a real position in Meccan trade. A merchant travelling north left someone with authority over his goods, his debts and his household. That man answered for what happened while he was away. The role carried power and risk together. To say he is not that for them told the audience exactly which relationship was not on offer.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a settled resting place in this ayah turns up elsewhere in the Quran. It is used for the earth as a dwelling and for the sun's course. So it belongs to the language of things reaching their appointed position. Applied to news, it treats a report as something travelling toward a place, rather than merely being true or false.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Responsibility is divided cleanly. The message is delivered. The answer belongs to those who receive it, and the timing belongs to God. That division is what makes long, unrewarded work bearable, and the Quran gives it to a messenger before anyone else. The second ayah adds the piece that makes trust possible. The ending is located, not merely promised. It has somewhere to arrive.

crossReferences.why: Draws the same line: whoever is guided is guided for himself, and he is not a keeper over them.
States the limit of the office in two clauses: you are a reminder, and not one who controls them.
Repeats the release if they turn away, since he was not sent as a guardian over them.

studies.applyIt: Pick something you have been carrying that belongs to someone else: a decision, a habit, a life you cannot live for them. Say the sentence out loud, that you are not the keeper of this. Then name the one part that is genuinely yours and do that. Setting a thing down properly requires knowing what remains in your hands.
studies.explainEasier: His own people said no to the message, and it is still the truth. He is told to say that he is not in charge of them. Every piece of news has a time when it lands, and they will find out.

studies.title: Until They Change The Subject
studies.meaning: The instruction is unusually practical. When people are wading into talk about God's signs, withdraw. The condition for coming back is stated exactly: until they move to another topic. Early scholars note that no argument is called for, and no confrontation. Then room is made for forgetting, which assumes it will happen. The second ayah frees the one who withdraws from any account for the others. It gives the whole instruction a purpose that is about them, not against them.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The setting is social rather than formal. People mocked the recitation in gatherings where believers were present, sometimes for fun. The classical scholars describe believers being drawn into defending the Quran in rooms where nothing was being decided. This ayah speaks to that. A Medinan passage later repeats the instruction in almost the same terms.

keyTerms.note: The verb for walking into water without knowing its depth. Used of talk, it names the kind of confident discussion that goes further than anybody's knowledge, which is why the Quran picks it for careless speech about God.
The same verb used earlier in this surah for those who turned from the signs. Here it is given as an instruction, so a word describing a fault becomes, in a different setting, a discipline.
Used twice in this passage with two senses: the recollection that ends forgetfulness, and the reminder offered to others. One word covers remembering yourself and being remembered to.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan evenings were spent in company. Men gathered by the sanctuary or in a courtyard and talk moved through poetry, news and jokes, with reputations made and lost by what someone said well. Leaving such a gathering was noticed. The instruction here has a social cost built into it, which is why the ayah names the exact condition under which you can sit back down.
studies.didYouKnow: This instruction appears twice in the Quran. Once here, in a Meccan surah, and once later in a Medinan one. Both use the same verb for wading into talk and the same condition about waiting for another subject. The Medinan version adds a clause about becoming like them, which the earlier version leaves unsaid.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats company as shaping, not neutral. Where you sit shapes what you get used to hearing. The remedy offered is physical distance, not a better argument. It also allows for human weakness with grace. Forgetting is expected, and answered with an instruction for afterwards rather than a telling off. And the purpose stays pointed at the others. The reminder is offered in hope, not in judgement.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same instruction in a Medinan setting, with the same condition about waiting for another topic.
Describes those who pass by empty talk with dignity, as a settled quality rather than a single choice.
Shows the same withdrawal from idle speech, with a courteous parting rather than a quarrel.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next conversation, online or in a room, where people are being clever about something sacred and nobody knows much. You do not need to correct anyone. Leave, or close the tab, and come back when the subject has changed. The ayah gives a condition for returning, which makes this a pause rather than a rupture.
studies.explainEasier: When people start making fun of God's words, walk away until they talk about something else. If you forget and stay, get up once you remember. Good people are not answerable for them. It is only a reminder.

studies.title: Religion As A Pastime
studies.meaning: Two words describe what has been done with religion. It has become play and pastime. Early scholars read this as covering both those who mocked and those who kept the forms without weight. The instruction is to leave them, and it is followed at once by an instruction to keep reminding. So withdrawal is not abandonment. The reason given is the danger of a soul being handed over to what it earned, with no ally, no one to speak for it, and no ransom accepted however much is offered.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The passage is about who can be reached, and how. The city's religious life was truly festive: seasonal fairs, poetry contests, rites around the sanctuary that doubled as show and trade. Calling that play and pastime was not a stretch invented for the argument. It named the set-up the city itself would have known.

keyTerms.note: Activity done for its own amusement, the word used of children's games. Applied to religion it says the practice is real and the seriousness is missing, which is a sharper charge than hypocrisy.
From a root for being taken in by an appearance, used of a market deal that looked better than it was. The deceiver is named as the present life itself rather than any person.

keyTerms.gloss: it is given up, handed over
keyTerms.note: A rare verb, appearing only in this ayah in the Quran, twice. Commentators gloss it as being consigned or held in pledge, and the range of their explanations reflects how uncommon the word is.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Ransom was an ordinary deal. A captive taken in a raid was priced and bought back. A killing could be settled with an agreed number of camels rather than blood. Every family knew the sums, and most had used them. The line saying no equivalent will be accepted removes the one device the audience relied on for undoing what could not be undone.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb describing a soul being handed over occurs nowhere else in the Quran. It appears twice, both times in this ayah. Rare words like this are the ones the earliest works on Quranic language worked hardest to explain. The commentaries keep several proposed meanings side by side.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Seriousness is treated as part of what religion is. So keeping the shape while dropping the weight is a change in kind, not a matter of degree. The passage also finishes the surah's argument about go-betweens by shutting the last door, which is payment. Nothing can be put in a person's place at that point. What a life actually contained is the only thing left.

crossReferences.why: Names the present life as play, amusement and adornment, then shows what remains of it.
Uses the same verb of deception, warning against being taken in by the present life and by the deceiver.
States the same refusal of ransom: an earth-full of gold would not be accepted from one of them.

studies.applyIt: Ask yourself what part of your religious life has become comfortable enough to be a routine you enjoy rather than something you mean. Not to give it up. Pick one such practice this week and do it slowly enough to notice what it is for. The ayah is about weight going missing while the shape remains.
studies.explainEasier: Some people treat religion as a game and a way to pass the time. Leave them alone, but keep reminding. On that day nobody can help a soul or pay anything to buy it back.

studies.title: Turned Back On Our Heels
studies.meaning: You are being urged back toward what you left behind. The reply is about direction, not argument. There is no sense in calling on something that can neither help nor harm you, then turning back on your heels after God has guided you. Turning back is a body moving in reverse, not a mind changing its view. A picture follows: a man drawn off by devils, lost in open country, while friends on the road call him to come. Early scholars notice that we never learn whether he answers. He is left there, and the answer closes: God's guidance is the guidance.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, and the pressure behind these words was real. People who accepted the message were being urged back by their own families, who framed the return as the reasonable thing and as loyalty to their own. What the verse answers is that framing, not the beliefs themselves. No specific occasion is attested for it. The surah comes back to this same situation in several places, using a different image each time.

keyTerms.note: The plural of heel, used in the idiom for turning back the way you came. It makes reversal a bodily movement, which is why the Quran uses it for abandoning a position rather than for changing a view.
A verb built on the root for falling and for desire, carrying both at once. The luring it describes is a downward pull toward what the person already wanted, not a snatching by something outside.
An intensive form for someone turning in place, unable to choose a direction. It appears only here in the whole Quran, and it names confusion as a physical state rather than a mental one.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Getting lost was the standard nightmare of desert travel, and the stories about it were exact. A man leaves the fire to check on an animal. By morning he has circled all night within a mile of the camp, while people called his name. Sound carries strangely over dunes, so voices could be near and still be no help. The scene here, with companions calling from the road and a man turning in place, was a story everyone had heard told.
studies.didYouKnow: One word in this verse, the one for the bewildered man, appears nowhere else in the Quran. Single uses like that are rare enough that classical scholars made lists of them. They tend to turn up at the vivid centre of a comparison, right where a plainer word would have blurred the picture.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Guidance is spoken of as a position you already hold, not a conclusion you are still weighing. That changes what leaving it would mean. The comparison also says something about how people get lost: they are not seized, they are drawn by something they wanted, and help is audible the whole time. Then the standard moves. Guidance is defined by its source, so the question stops being which road feels right.

crossReferences.why: States the same measure in almost identical words, that God's guidance is the guidance itself.
Describes people who took devils as allies instead of God and reckon they are guided.
Pictures the reversal differently, as worship on an edge that turns away when trouble comes.

studies.applyIt: Think of a good practice you have quietly let go of in the last year, and notice how the letting go was argued for at the time. It usually sounds reasonable. Pick that one thing and restart it this week at half its old size. This verse describes reversal as movement, which means it can be walked back the same way.
studies.explainEasier: They are asked why they would call on something that cannot help them or hurt them. God has already guided them. Turning back would be like a man led away by devils. He wanders lost while his friends call him.

studies.title: And To Establish The Prayer
studies.meaning: Prayer is the first thing most people let slip when life gets heavy. These words finish a thought that began with surrender to the Lord of the worlds, and they add two things: keep the prayer standing, and stay mindful of Him. Early scholars note that the verb here does not mean simply to perform the prayer. It means to set something upright and keep it that way, like a tent you put up and then keep from falling. The words at the end give the reason. It is to Him that you will be gathered.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, in the first years. The prayer in view here is the early one, before the fuller detail that came later in Medina. The classical sources say regular prayer sat at the centre of Meccan believers' lives from very early on. It was also what got them hurt. Much of the harassment they met came when someone saw them praying. So an instruction to keep the prayer standing was, at that moment, an instruction to keep standing where people could see you.

keyTerms.note: The causative of standing. It is used for putting up a building and for keeping an institution going, so it asks for a prayer held upright over time rather than one simply carried out.
From a root meaning to guard or shield yourself. It describes careful attention to a relationship rather than fear of a person, which is why the English words piety and fear both fall short of it.
The same passive used earlier in this surah for being assembled before God. Its return here ties the two instructions to a destination instead of leaving them as good practice.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Standing in prayer was hard to hide in Mecca. There was no separate building for it and no privacy. People prayed in courtyards, at the edge of the sanctuary, out in the open where anyone walking past could see them. Some of the early believers went out to the ravines around the city so they could pray unwatched. In a place like that, keeping the prayer standing was a public commitment, which is what the words here ask for.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran almost never says simply to do the prayer. It nearly always pairs it with the verb for setting something upright, and the pattern holds across Meccan and Medinan passages alike. Early grammar writers noticed how steady it was and treated the pairing as fixed. The effect is that prayer stays something you keep going, not something you get through.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Prayer is put here as the practical shape of surrender, not as an extra on top of it. The belief and the daily standing are named in one breath, and that link matters more than either on its own. The mention of being gathered sets the frame around both. Prayer is not offered here as a method for a better life now. It is the ordinary posture of someone who expects to stand somewhere one day and answer.

crossReferences.why: Gives the prayer a purpose in the same command form, as a way of remembering God.
Says what the practice does over time, holding a person back from what is shameful and wrong.
Sets the prayer at both ends of the day, with good deeds clearing away what is bad.

studies.applyIt: Pick the prayer in your day that is most rushed, usually the one squeezed against something else. Give it five extra minutes tomorrow. Not more words, just room around it, so that the standing is not followed straight away by moving. The verb here is about keeping something upright, and things stay upright when nothing knocks into them.
studies.explainEasier: Keep the prayer going, and keep God in mind. That is what the words say here. In the end everyone is brought together in front of Him.

studies.title: His Word Is The Truth
studies.meaning: Everything you can see was made on purpose, and this verse says so in one phrase. God created the heavens and the earth in truth, which means with purpose rather than as a game. Then comes how: He says be, and it is. Early scholars notice the tense here, because a day still ahead is described with a present verb. That keeps one act of command over both the first creation and the raising to come. And rule on the day the trumpet is blown is named as His alone.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. This verse sits in a stretch of the surah that runs through Abraham's argument with his own people and then a list of prophets. The people listening already agreed that God made the world. What they did was treat other powers as go-betweens who could get things done for them. The answer here leaves no room for a second authority on the day it would matter most. Early scholars report no particular occasion for it.

keyTerms.note: The word covers truth, right, and what is due. Saying the heavens were made with it denies that creation is arbitrary, and the same word returns a moment later to describe God's own speech.
The bare command form of the verb to be, two letters in Arabic. It is the shortest order the language can make, and the shortness is the point: nothing stands between the intention and the thing.

A curved horn of the kind used to call people together or signal an army. The Quran uses it for the blast that ends everything and then restarts it, and here it fixes the moment when rule becomes undeniable.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Power in Mecca was shared out among the clans, partly by office and partly by custom. Nobody held all of it. Choices were made in council, alliances shifted, and the man on top one season could be beaten the next. A claim that rule on one day belongs to a single holder, with no council and no haggling, described something nobody there had ever seen.
studies.didYouKnow: The command that brings a thing into being is two letters long in Arabic. It appears several times in the Quran, always in the same construction, and the answer always comes in the same breath. There is no gap at all between the order and the result. The grammar itself refuses to allow an interval in which the thing might not yet exist.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Creation and resurrection are folded into one kind of act here. If the first needed nothing but a word, the second cannot be harder, and that argument is made without ever being stated. Calling God the knower of what is hidden and what is seen then closes a gap a listener might have used. No corner of a life, private or public, sits outside the same authority. And the names at the end are about wisdom and fine detail, not about force.

crossReferences.why: States the same command and the answer that follows at once, arguing directly for the raising of the dead.
Applies the same wording to the bringing into being of the heavens and the earth.
Describes the two blasts of the trumpet and what happens between them.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you keep postponing because the first step feels heavy. Do the smallest possible version of it in the next hour, not the whole thing. This verse puts no distance at all between a word and its effect. Nothing human works that way, but most of the distance we feel turns out to be added by us.
studies.explainEasier: God made the sky and the earth for a reason. When He says to a thing, be, it is. On the day the trumpet sounds, everything will belong to Him alone.

studies.title: Do You Take Idols As Gods
studies.meaning: Sometimes the hardest person to disagree with is the one who raised you. Abraham puts his question to his own father, and it is not an attack. It sounds more like disbelief that anyone could take carved figures for gods. Then he says what he sees, using the word for plain, visible error, and he includes the whole community in it. The next words pull back and explain what is really happening. God was showing him the dominion of the heavens and the earth, so that he would be one of those who are certain. What follows is teaching, then, not wavering.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. This comes right after words about being called back by your own people, and the join is not an accident. Abraham's position matched exactly what the early Meccan community faced. He was a man breaking with the religion of his own household, which was what many of them were doing. The scholars discuss the name given here for his father. Some take it as his name, others as a title or a second name, and they leave the difference standing rather than settling it.

keyTerms.note: Shaped figures, kept distinct in Arabic usage from unshaped stones that were also set up for worship. The word points at manufacture, which is exactly what the question to his father turns on.
A strengthened form of the word for kingdom, and it appears only a few times in the Quran. It names not the things owned but the fact of their being held, which is what he is shown.
From a root for knowledge that has settled and stopped moving. It names a state rather than an act, and it is given here as the intended outcome of what he is about to be shown.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Breaking with your father's religion in that world cost you a household, a name and a trade all at once. Religion was not a private choice there. It was the property of a family line, kept by the same people who kept the wells and the grazing rights. The Meccan converts hearing this story had made the same break, or were about to. The passage names the one person it costs most to face.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for dominion used here is never used in the Quran for ordinary kingship. It turns up only a handful of times, and it carries a strengthening ending that Arabic uses sparingly. Its rarity marks what Abraham is shown as a different kind of seeing. He is not simply looking at the sky more carefully than usual.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Certainty is described as something shown to a person, not argued into place. That frames the sequence with the star, the moon and the sun as a lesson rather than a wavering faith. The passage also says that the search can begin by standing against what you were raised in. And it says that standing against it can still be done with respect. Abraham asks his father a question before he announces any conclusion to anyone.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same conversation at length, with its gentleness and its repeated address to his father.
Shows him pressing the question further, asking about the images his people are devoted to.
Preserves his declaration that he disowns what they worship, apart from the One who made him.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you believe mainly because it was in the house you grew up in. It can be small: a view about money, a way of handling conflict. Ask once where it came from, without deciding anything about it. This passage begins with a question rather than a rejection, and the question is the part worth copying.
studies.explainEasier: Abraham asked his father why he treated carved statues as gods. He said his father and their people were clearly wrong. God then showed Abraham how the sky and the earth are held, so he would be sure.

studies.theme: The Love Between God and the Believer
studies.title: I Do Not Love What Sets
studies.meaning: Night falls, and a bright star comes out. Abraham does his thinking out loud, and the conclusion arrives with a verb of love rather than of logic. He looks up and says this is my Lord. Then the star goes down, and he says he does not love the things that set. Early scholars differ over whether he is working his own way forward or arguing with his people on their own terms. Both readings are old. Either way, the test he applies is attachment, and setting is what fails it.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, in the middle of an argument about what deserves worship. Star and planet worship was practised across the wider region and was known in Arabia, so the sequence begins with a real option rather than an imagined one. That matters for how you read it. The classical scholars treat this stage as the first move of a demonstration. It is not a report that Abraham ever believed it.

keyTerms.note: A verb for covering over, from the root that gives the words for a garden, a hidden being and the inner chamber of the heart. Night arrives here as a covering laid over him, not as light leaving.
A bright body in the sky, used in Arabic for the wandering ones as well as the fixed. It is left unnamed here, so the argument does not depend on which one it was.
A word for a body sinking below the horizon, and beyond that for anything that fades and disappears. It is the hinge of the whole sequence, coming back at every stage.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: People in Arabia found their way by the stars, and they tracked risings and settings closely enough to fix the seasons and time a journey. Herdsmen and guides could name individual stars and knew which ones appeared when. To that audience, a body that sets was not a poetic idea at all. It was a working fact used every night, and its regularity was exactly what made it useful.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for nightfall here shares its root with three other Arabic words, and the company it keeps is surprising. One is the word for a garden. One names the unseen beings the Quran mentions elsewhere. One is the sheltered inner part of a person. All of them are covered or hidden from view, so a single set of letters ties hiddenness to what is inside.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Love is brought in as a test for what may be worshipped, which is unusual in a surah built on argument. What sets cannot be loved rightly, because attachment to something that goes under has its ending built in. The test also reaches well past idols. Anything that reliably departs, including status and strength, fails it. That is why people still remember this sequence far outside the setting it came from.

crossReferences.why: Continues the sequence with the moon, adding a plea for guidance when it too disappears.
Draws the same conclusion directly: do not bow to the sun or moon, but to the One who made them.
Turns the test around, describing love that runs from God toward the one who follows the way.

studies.applyIt: Name one thing you are attached to right now that you know will not last: a role, a physical capacity, a season of life you are inside. Do not try to detach from it. Just say clearly to yourself that it sets. This passage does not ask for coldness. It asks you to know which things are on their way down before they go.
studies.explainEasier: When night came, Abraham saw a star and said, this is my lord. Then it went down, and he said he does not love things that set and disappear.

studies.title: Unless My Lord Guides Me
studies.meaning: The moon comes up, brighter than the star, and the same thing happens again. He names it his Lord, and then it sets. This time he does not say anything about love. He says something about himself: without his Lord's guidance he would be one of the people who go astray. Early scholars note the step up. He has moved from weighing an object to seeing how exposed he is, and what he says is a condition rather than a confident claim. The thinking has produced a prayer before it has produced a conclusion.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. This is the middle of three scenes the surah presents as teaching given to Abraham. Across the ancient Near East the moon carried more religious weight than any single star did. So this stage raises the stakes on the one before it, and his hearers would have felt that. The scholars treat the whole sequence as a demonstration put on for his people. It is not a record of a belief he actually held.

keyTerms.note: A word for something breaking into view, used of the moon and the sun coming up. The root carries a sense of splitting through, so the rising is pictured as an emergence rather than a smooth arrival.
A conditional particle that carries an oath, so what follows it is sworn rather than supposed. It turns the admission he makes into a solemn statement instead of a passing thought.
The same root used through this surah for losing a road, and for what the invented partners do in the end. Applying it to himself puts him in the very group he has been describing in others.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The lunar month organised everything. Arabs dated debts, fairs, journeys and the sacred months by the phases of the moon, and a new crescent sighted from a rooftop began a month for a whole region. It was the most important object in the sky for daily life. So watching it set was not a small observation. It was watching the timekeeper of the year go under.
studies.didYouKnow: The three scenes climb in brightness: a star, then the moon, then the sun. Each one ends differently. First comes a statement about love, then a plea for guidance, and last a declaration. The build is deliberate, and the middle stage is the only one of the three that is a prayer.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Certainty turns out to include a moment of dependence. The very figure the Quran holds up as the model of finding God says he would go astray without being guided. And he says it after reasoning correctly, not before. That puts asking at the centre of the search rather than at its start. It also makes fear and hope work together here. The fear names a real possibility, and turning to God makes it into a request.

crossReferences.why: Turns the same request into the daily prayer of everyone who recites it, in almost the same words.
Gives the stage before this one, where the test applied to the setting star was love rather than a plea.
Records a similar phrase, hoping the Lord will guide to what is nearer than this to right conduct.

studies.applyIt: Take a decision you are close to making, and add one sentence before you decide. Say that you could get this wrong and would like to be guided. Say it as a request, not as a formality. This passage puts the plea in the middle of good reasoning, not in place of it. The middle is where most of us leave it out.
studies.explainEasier: Next Abraham saw the moon coming up and said, this is my lord. When it set too, he said that without God guiding him he would be one of the people who lose their way.

studies.title: When The Sun Went Down
studies.meaning: The sun comes up, the biggest thing in the sky, and the sequence ends. Abraham has watched a star, then the moon, then the sun, calling each one his lord and then stepping back when it set. Early scholars differ over what he was doing. Some read it as his own search for God. Others read it as an argument with his people, in which he takes up their assumption and follows it until it falls apart. Either way, the conclusion is not that the sun is small. It is that whatever sets cannot be what he is looking for.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. Much of this surah is an argument with people who worshipped God and other powers together. Abraham is brought in because he was the ancestor they claimed. Early scholars point out how sharp that is. The city traced its bloodline and its sanctuary back to him, and here he is shown rejecting the very arrangement his descendants had settled into. No particular occasion is reported for the passage.

keyTerms.note: A word for something bursting into view, used of dawn and of blood from a wound. It gives the appearance of the sun a suddenness that makes its later setting all the more pointed.
A legal term for being clear of a debt or a charge. Using it here makes the break formal rather than emotional, the way a man publicly renounces a liability he will not carry.
One who turns away from the practice around him toward what is upright. The Quran uses it again and again of Abraham, and it describes a direction taken rather than a doctrine held.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Star religion was familiar across Arabia and the lands nearby. Some tribes were linked with particular heavenly bodies, and caravans steered by the same stars they called on. Anyone travelling at night knew the order of risings and settings by heart. Abraham's argument works because his hearers were expert watchers. They knew better than anyone that everything in that sky goes down.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of very few places in the Quran that lays out a line of reasoning step by step. The conclusion arrives at the end instead of being announced at the start. Classical scholars disagree about what it records. Some read it as Abraham's own search, others as a method of debate, and major authorities have held both readings.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The test he applies is what goes away: whatever cannot stay is ruled out. That test is open to anyone with patience and a horizon. It needs no book and no teacher. The passage also shows a public break with the practice you were raised in, which is costly in any group built on family line. And what he declares at the end is about direction, a face turned one way, rather than about agreeing to a statement.

crossReferences.why: Gives the earlier steps of the same sequence, the star and then the moon.
Tells the other Abraham story, the broken idols and the question put to his people.
Shows him arguing about a lord who gives life, with the sun brought into it again.

studies.applyIt: Take something you rely on for a sense of stability: a job, one person's approval, a number in an account. Ask what happens to your footing if it goes, and answer honestly rather than bravely. Abraham's test was not contempt for what he was watching. It was noticing what those things do at the end of the day.
studies.explainEasier: Abraham watched a star, then the moon, then the sun. Each one rose and then went down again. So he told his people that none of them could be his lord. He turned instead to the One who made the sky and the earth.

studies.title: My Lord Encompasses All Things
studies.meaning: His people crowd in to argue, and he does not argue back. He asks why they are disputing with him about God when God has already guided him. That moves the disagreement onto different ground, because he is not offering a theory to be weighed against theirs. Then he answers the threat sitting behind their argument. He does not fear what they associate with God, and the only exception he allows is what his Lord wills, so even his own safety is not claimed as his. The reason comes last: his Lord's knowledge takes in everything.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, and the exchange matches a pressure the early community knew well. Warnings that abandoned gods would take revenge were part of how households kept their members in line. The sources describe converts being told they would be struck with illness or bad luck. Abraham's answer here meets that kind of argument rather than an intellectual one, which is why it turns on fear rather than on proof.

keyTerms.note: From the root for a proof or an argument, in a form that means trading arguments back and forth. It names the activity rather than the content, and the activity is what he is declining to continue.
A verb for holding something with room to spare, used of a vessel bigger than what is poured into it. Applied to knowledge, it says nothing overflows and nothing falls outside.
A form of remembering that means fetching back what you already hold, not learning something new. It assumes his listeners have what they need and are simply not consulting it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Fear of an offended local god was practical, not abstract. A tribe would blame a drought, a stillbirth or a lost caravan on a shrine neglected or an oath broken. That thinking drove real choices about where to travel and what to sacrifice. Telling a family you had left their god was, to them, news that you had put the whole household in danger.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here for encompassing is the one that names the widest verse in the Quran, the verse about the seat that reaches over the heavens and the earth. The same root gives Arabic its word for spaciousness and for being at ease. Knowledge and roominess, in other words, share a single set of letters.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are held together here that usually come apart. He says he does not fear what they worship, and in the same breath adds a condition, so even his fearlessness is not treated as his own. Nothing at all is claimed for himself. The passage also treats guidance as a change in where you stand, not a change of opinion. That is why a debate is no longer the right shape for the conversation. He is reporting something he was given, not defending a position he chose.

crossReferences.why: Records another dispute with Abraham about his Lord, and how that argument was closed.
Puts the same challenge to his people about worshipping what neither benefits nor harms them.
Uses nearly identical wording about a Lord whose knowledge encompasses everything there is.

studies.applyIt: Notice an argument you keep re-entering with someone who has no intention of moving. Ask what you are actually defending, and whether carrying on serves it. You can leave a dispute without leaving the person or the position. The speaker here states his ground, gives his reason, asks one question, and stops.
studies.explainEasier: His people argued with him about God. He asked why, when God had already guided him. He said he is not afraid of the things they worship. His Lord knows everything there is.

studies.title: Which Side Deserves Security
studies.meaning: Someone has just threatened Abraham with the anger of their gods, and he turns the threat around. He asks who should really be afraid of whom. They have attached partners to God with nothing sent down to warrant it, and he has not. Then he leaves the question of which side has more right to safety hanging for them to answer. The next verse gives the answer: those who believe and do not cloud their faith with wrongdoing. That condition is what early scholars discuss most.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, with Abraham's dispute still running, just after he disowned what his people worshipped. The surah lays that exchange over its own audience. The Meccans had warned the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) that their gods might strike him down. The classical sources also keep reports of early listeners who were troubled by the second of these two verses. They heard the word for wrongdoing in its widest sense and feared it covered them.

keyTerms.note: A word for a sanction or proof that gives someone the right to act, and later for a ruler. Its use here asks for a warrant: the practice is challenged because nothing was ever issued behind it.
From the same root as faith and trust. The word for being safe and the word for believing come from one source, which is why these verses can move between them without changing subject.
A verb for clothing something or covering it over, used of confusing truth with falsehood. Faith is pictured as a garment that can be worn with something else layered on top of it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Fear of offending a tribal god was practical, not theoretical. Shrines were credited with causing illness, drought or a failed journey when they were slighted, and people arranged their travel and their oaths around that. Threatening someone with the anger of a god was a real threat in that world. Abraham's reply does not deny that the fear is reasonable. It asks which of the two sides is actually exposed.
studies.didYouKnow: The Arabic word for security and the Arabic word for faith grow from the same root. Both of them stand in the same sentence as this passage closes. That lets the point land through sound as well as through sense. A listener hears the link between believing and being safe before the argument has been spelled out.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Safety is presented as something that follows from what is true, not from what is powerful. The question about which side has more right to it assumes that security follows accuracy. A person lined up with reality stands differently from one who is not, whoever happens to be frightened at the moment. Then the condition keeps this from turning smug. Faith is described as something that can be clouded over.

crossReferences.why: Names associating partners with God as a great wrong, which is the reading given to this passage.
Comes just before, where his people dispute with him and he refuses to fear.
Describes God as the ally of believers, bringing them out of darkness into light.

studies.applyIt: Name one thing you are quietly afraid of that has been shaping your decisions this month. Then put Abraham's question to it: what is it actually able to do, and on whose authority. You are not talking yourself out of the fear. You are checking whether it has the standing you have been giving it.
studies.explainEasier: Abraham asks his people why he should fear their gods, when they are not afraid of setting up gods beside God with no proof at all. He asks which side is really safe. The answer is those who believe and do no wrong.

studies.title: That Was Our Argument
studies.meaning: You have just watched a man reason his way to God, and now you are told where the reasoning came from. It was Our argument, given to Abraham. Early scholars take that as covering both the seeing described earlier and the words he actually spoke. Then the statement widens out: God raises in degrees whomever He wills. The two names that follow keep the raising from looking like a whim, since it is done by One who is wise and fully informed. What looked like a private achievement is handed back without being made smaller.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. This closes the Abraham story, just before the surah turns to the line of prophets who came after him. The story has been answering people who argued that the religion they inherited needed no defence. Here the words turn to the listeners directly and say your Lord. That pulls the argument out of the past and lays it in front of the people hearing it.

keyTerms.note: A word for a decisive case in a dispute, the kind that ends it. Assigning it to God rather than to Abraham is the whole point, since the reasoning was received and not invented.
Steps of a stair, used for gradations of standing. The plural and its indefinite form leave both the number and the measure open, so no ranking scale is offered to the reader.
From a root for restraining and for sound judgement, the same one that gives the word for a bridle. Wisdom in Arabic includes holding back, which is why it pairs so naturally with knowing everything.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Skill in argument was prized and taught. A man who could carry a case before the assembly protected his family's interests, and the language of proof and reply was familiar to anyone who had watched a dispute settled in public. Handing a winning argument to someone else was unusual there. A good case was a personal credit, much like a good poem.
studies.didYouKnow: The line about raising in degrees turns up elsewhere in the Quran, and there it is tied to knowledge. That passage adds that above everyone with knowledge stands one who knows more. So the same phrase does duty twice, once for a prophet's reasoning and once for the ordinary ranks of learning.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Insight is given rather than earned, and that unsettles a pride most of us feel naturally. The sequence with the star, the moon and the sun reads like a mind at work. These words say the working itself was a gift. That does not make the effort unreal, but it changes what a person can take credit for. The names at the end guard the whole thing from feeling like a whim, since raising is done knowingly and with judgement, not by preference.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the line about raising in degrees and adds that every knower has one above him.
States the same thing plainly, that Abraham's soundness of judgement was given to him beforehand.
Applies the raising in degrees to believers and to those who have been given knowledge.

studies.applyIt: Think of a good idea you had recently and try to trace where it actually came from: a conversation, a book, a mood, a night of decent sleep. You will not find a clean origin. Sitting with that for a minute is what this passage proposes, and it makes the credit harder to hold and easier to carry.
studies.explainEasier: That whole argument was given to Abraham by God. It was not something he worked out on his own. God lifts whoever He wants to a higher place. Your Lord is wise and knows everything.

studies.title: Each Of Them We Guided
studies.meaning: A list of names begins, and it does not run by date. Isaac and Jacob come first, given to Abraham as a gift. Then Noah is mentioned as earlier, and after him a run of names described as from his descendants. Early scholars discuss whether that word points back to Abraham or to Noah, and both readings are old and defensible. The refrain does the real work: each of them We guided. Repeating it means the credit is placed the same way every time, and the words at the end name them all as people who do good.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, and this follows straight on from the Abraham sequence, in a city that valued lineage above almost everything. Mecca's leading families traced their descent from Abraham through Ishmael and used it as a claim to standing. The list here runs through that same ancestry, but it measures it by guidance rather than by blood. That quietly changes what an inheritance is.

keyTerms.note: A verb for giving with no payment and no return, the root behind the Arabic word for a gift. The Quran uses it for children in particular, which places offspring outside anything earned.

A collective noun for what issues from someone, linked by early Arabic dictionary writers to scattering seed. It covers a whole line rather than a generation, which is what lets one word carry the entire list.
From a root for beauty and excellence, so the word means doing something well rather than merely doing it. Naming the prophets this way measures them by the quality of what they did, not by rank.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Genealogy was the memory system of Arabia. Men could recite their ancestry back many generations, and arguments over precedence were settled by who could name a longer or better line. Poets were paid to keep it. A list of weighty names was therefore a familiar kind of speech to this audience, and they would have heard this one as a claim about who the real ancestors are.
studies.didYouKnow: This verse and the two after it name seventeen prophets in one unbroken run, the longest such list anywhere in the Quran. The order follows neither the dates nor the alphabet. Classical scholars noticed that it groups figures by kinship and by kind instead. Relatives are placed beside one another rather than in order of century.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Guidance is named as the one thing shared across an enormously varied set of lives. The list holds a king, a fugitive, a prisoner and a man who preached for centuries. Nothing else in it is shared at all. That makes the repeated refrain the real claim of the passage. What these people had in common was not their circumstances and not their success. It was the same thing being given to each of them.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same gift to Abraham of Isaac and, on top of that, Jacob, each made upright.
Places prophethood and the Book within his descendants, which is what this list then traces.
Gives a parallel list of those to whom revelation was sent, overlapping with this one a great deal.

studies.applyIt: Pick one of the names in this list you know least about and read a short account of that prophet this week. Most readers have three or four they know well and the rest as names only. Filling in one changes how the list reads. It stops being a recitation and starts being people whose lives went very differently.
studies.explainEasier: God gave Abraham Isaac and Jacob, and guided them both. He had guided Noah before that. From the same line came David, Solomon, Job, Joseph, Moses and Aaron. That is how God rewards people who do good.

studies.title: Their Fathers And Their Brothers
studies.meaning: The list of names keeps going, and then the last line opens outward in three directions at once: their ancestors, their descendants, and their brothers. Early scholars note that these words refuse, on purpose, to draw a line around the group. Not every relative is included. The word used means some of them, and sons are not the only ones named. The passage ends with two verbs, chosen and guided, and both describe what was done rather than who deserved it.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, and this sits inside the longest run of prophetic names in the Quran. The audience included people from the scriptural communities of the region as well as Meccans. Several of these names belonged to traditions the Meccans knew only at second hand. Naming them all together in one breath makes a claim. There is one line of guidance behind traditions the region had come to treat as separate.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to be fit or in good working order, used of a mended wall or a workable arrangement. Uprightness in Arabic is soundness rather than sanctity, which keeps the word ordinary.
An intensive verb from the root for surplus, for what is left over. Favour here is something extra given rather than a merit recognised, which fits a passage where everything is credited to God.
A verb for gathering something up and picking it out, used of collecting the best of a crop. It implies choosing from among many rather than finding the only candidate there was.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian families were wide and layered. They took in brothers, half-brothers, cousins raised as siblings, and adopted members who took the family name. A household had one shared identity, and honour or shame travelled through the whole of it. Against that background, saying that only some of the fathers, descendants and brothers were chosen is a strange claim. In that world a family line carried the whole family together.
studies.didYouKnow: The list places relatives side by side instead of following the centuries. Moses and Aaron close the verse before this one, as brothers. This passage opens with Zechariah followed at once by John, a father and his son. The last line then makes the rule plain, by naming ancestors, descendants and brothers together.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates family line from being chosen, while running the two along the same track. Prophethood is given inside families again and again, and it is never given to a family as such. That distinction protects two things at once. Inherited faith is real, and the Quran treats it as a genuine advantage. It also confers nothing on its own. Being related to guidance is not the same as receiving it.

crossReferences.why: Names families chosen above the worlds, describing them as descendants issuing one from another.
Gathers many of these same figures as those God favoured, from several distinct lines of descent.
States that prophethood was placed in the descendants of Noah and Abraham, with mixed results.

studies.applyIt: Think of the faith you inherited from your family and name one thing in it that came to you already made, that you never had to build. It might be a habit of prayer, or simply the assumption that God is there. Say what it is, and thank whoever passed it down, aloud if they are still reachable.
studies.explainEasier: The list goes on with Zechariah, John, Jesus and Elias, then Ishmael, Elijah, Jonah and Lot. God chose them and set them above everyone else. He chose some of their fathers, children and brothers too, and led them on a straight road.

studies.title: Such Is God's Guidance
studies.meaning: The long list ends, and the whole of it is summed up in three words: such is God's guidance. He gives it to whomever He wills among His servants. Then comes a condition that lands hard. Had even these figures set others beside God, everything they did would have collapsed. Early scholars note how much force there is in applying that to prophets. It is not a warning aimed at them. It says that nothing in the list was made safe by the standing of the people in it.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, at the close of a passage that ran right through the prophetic line. The Meccans accepted a supreme God and added others alongside Him. The surah has been arguing that adding them is not a small adjustment. Putting this at the end of the list applies the argument at its strongest point, to the very figures both sides respected.

keyTerms.note: A vivid verb, used of an animal that eats bad pasture and swells up before it dies. Work that comes to nothing is pictured as something that looks full and then fails, not as something small.
The same word this surah uses for all of humanity. Its use here, in a sentence about prophets, quietly keeps them inside the general category rather than lifting them out of it.
The verb of willing, left without qualification. The Quran uses it this way without giving a standard, and mainstream early scholars read that silence as deliberate rather than as something missing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Grazing was a constant calculation. A herd moved onto rich ground could bloat and die, and the swelling looked at first like the animal thriving. Herdsmen knew the sign and dreaded it, because the loss came exactly when the beast looked at its best. The verb here carries that picture, and the audience would have heard it before hearing anything abstract.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for deeds coming to nothing has a farmyard picture inside it. In the classical dictionaries its plain sense is a beast swelling from bad pasture. The Quran uses the verb more than a dozen times, almost always built the same way, about work made void. So a word about ruin carries a picture of ruin dressed up as plenty.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Everything the passage has described is placed under one condition, and the condition is applied to the highest subjects there are. Nothing here builds up a standing that could survive it. That is the central argument of the surah at its sharpest. Setting others beside God is not one fault among many. It is the thing that empties the rest. It also explains why a book so patient about most failings keeps returning to this one.

crossReferences.why: States the same condition directly to a messenger, that association would make his work worthless.
Describes what this guidance does, leading those who follow it out of darkness into light.
Shows deeds coming to nothing on the same principle, so no weight is given them at the reckoning.

studies.applyIt: Look at one good thing you do regularly and ask honestly what else is mixed into it: a reputation, a habit of being seen doing it, an obligation to someone watching. You do not have to purify it in an afternoon. Just find the mixture and know it is there. This passage says the mixture is what matters most.
studies.explainEasier: That is God's guidance, and He gives it to whoever He wants. Even these prophets were under the same rule. If they had set anything beside God, everything they did would have come to nothing.

studies.title: Entrusted To Another People
studies.meaning: Three things are named as given: the Book, sound judgement, and prophethood. Then a condition follows, and it reads less like a threat than like an observation about how this has always worked. If the people standing in front of you reject all this, it has already been entrusted to others who will not. Early scholars point to the tense. The verb is past, so the alternative is not a plan held in reserve. It has been done already.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. The rejection in view is the immediate one, coming from a city that had been hearing the recitation for years. The classical scholars differ over who exactly the people entrusted are. Some read it of the emigrants and helpers who would go on to form the community. Others read it more broadly, of anyone who receives it in any generation. The reading is left open.

keyTerms.note: From the root for restraining and deciding, covering wisdom in judging a matter. Placed between scripture and prophethood, it names the ability to apply a text rather than merely to receive one.
From the root for an agent put in charge of someone else's affairs. The same root is used earlier in this surah, when the Prophet is told he is not such an agent over anyone.
A demonstrative for people who are present and close at hand. It makes the sentence concrete, so the rejection being discussed belongs to the room rather than to a category of humanity.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Trades and offices passed within families, and they could also be lost. One clan held the keys to the sanctuary, another the right to water the pilgrims. These jobs were inherited, argued over, and now and then moved on when a line failed or fell out of favour. Everyone knew that such a charge could pass to another house. This passage uses that familiar machinery for something much larger.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for entrusting here shares a root with a word used a few pages earlier, and the pairing is striking. There the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) is told he is not a keeper over his people. So the same letters mark two things at once. They mark the duty he is released from, and the duty given to those who receive the message.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Revelation is described as never being at risk. Only its keepers are, and that moves the worry somewhere else. The question is not whether the message survives but who is carrying it, and the answer to that has changed before and can change again. The passage also offers an odd comfort to a small, pressured community. The handing on does not depend on the people who currently hold the standing.

crossReferences.why: Names the same three gifts, the Book, judgement and prophethood, given to an earlier community.
States the replacement plainly: turn away and others will be brought who are not like you.
Describes a people God will bring in place of those who turn back, loved by Him and loving Him.

studies.applyIt: Think of something valuable you are the current holder of: a family practice, a piece of knowledge, a role in a community. Ask who you are handing it to, and whether you have started. Nothing in this passage is about losing the thing itself. It is about who ends up carrying it, and that is decided by whoever bothers.
studies.explainEasier: Those are the people God gave the Book, good judgement and prophethood. The people here may turn all that down. If so, it has already been put in the care of others. Those others will not turn it down.

studies.title: I Ask You No Reward
studies.meaning: The instruction is to follow their guidance, and early scholars are careful about what that means. It is not to copy the particular laws given to earlier communities. It is to take the same road they were on, because the verse has just described that road as one thing. Then the words turn to the people listening, with a denial about money. Nothing is being charged for any of this. And the words at the end say what it is instead: a reminder, offered to everyone, with no deal attached.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, where the denial answered a live suspicion. Religious jobs in the city brought in money, from care of the sanctuary to fees for fortune-telling. A new claim about God was naturally read as a bid for a share of that. Several Meccan surahs record the same denial in almost the same words. So the suspicion kept coming back rather than arising once.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning a model or a standard, in a form that means taking someone as a pattern. Its last letter is a rare spelling feature that most reciters keep, marking the word as a stopping point.
The ordinary word for pay owed for work done, used of a hired labourer. Its plain commercial sense is what makes the denial concrete rather than pious.
Not new information but the bringing back of something already known. Describing the whole message this way limits the claim: what is offered is recollection rather than a novelty being sold.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca's religious trade was out in the open. Water rights for pilgrims, care of the sanctuary and the fairs around it brought income and standing to certain families. Poets and diviners were paid for their work. Anyone who spoke about the gods in that city was assumed to be angling for a share. That is the assumption these words step around by naming it.
studies.didYouKnow: Refusing payment is not personal modesty in the Quran. It is standard equipment for a messenger. The denial runs through the book in the mouths of many of them, always in similar words, and in one surah alone it is repeated five times by five different figures. That steadiness makes taking no money a feature of the office.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Taking no payment removes a motive, and the passage offers that as proof rather than as a boast. If nothing is being collected, the usual reason for why someone keeps going is simply gone. Calling the whole message a reminder makes a second point about what it holds. It claims to bring back something people already have, rather than to hand them a new system. That is why it can be offered to everyone, with nothing changed.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same two clauses almost word for word: no payment asked, and only a reminder to the worlds.
Gives the one exception ever named: that whoever wishes may take a way toward his Lord.
Puts the identical disclaimer in the mouth of an earlier messenger addressing his own people.

studies.applyIt: Pick something you do for others and check what you are quietly collecting for it: thanks, a reputation, the sense of being the reliable one. Do the same thing this week without any of that reaching you, if you can arrange it. Notice whether you still want to do it. That is the whole experiment this passage suggests.
studies.explainEasier: Those are the people God guided, so follow the way they took. The Prophet asks for no pay for any of this. It is only a reminder for everyone.

studies.title: They Did Not Value God
studies.meaning: The charge here is not disbelief so much as bad measuring. To say that God has never revealed anything to any human being is to underrate Him, because it denies that He can speak at all. The answer comes back as a question with a fact inside it. It asks who sent down the Book that Moses brought, the one called a light and a guidance. Then the handling of that Book is described, put onto sheets with some shown and much kept back. The instruction at the end is to say the answer and walk away.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. The classical scholars differ over who is being addressed in the middle of this verse. Some read the whole of it as aimed at Meccans who denied revelation outright. Others read it as turning to those who held the earlier scripture and handled it selectively. The shift between plural addressees in the Arabic is what produces the disagreement, and the tradition records both readings.

keyTerms.note: A verb for sizing something up, used of weighing a load or judging a distance. So the failing named is a mismeasurement rather than a denial, which is a subtler and far more common error.
The plural of the word used earlier in this surah for a writing sheet, and its only other appearance in the Quran. Both times it turns up inside these ninety verses.
The noun from the verb for wading into water of unknown depth. It was used a few verses earlier in this surah for careless talk about God's signs, and its return here closes a loop.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Scripture in that region existed as scrolls, kept by the communities who could read them. Access ran through the few people able to do so. A text was read aloud to a gathering by someone who chose the passage, and that was normal. It also gave real power to the reader. What was not read aloud did not exist for the people listening.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about not valuing God as He deserves appears three times in the Quran, always in exactly this form. Each time it introduces a different failure of judgement. Here it is the denial that God speaks to human beings at all. Elsewhere it comes just before descriptions of His power over creation on the day everyone is raised.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Denying revelation is treated as a claim about God, not as caution about what people claim. To say nothing has ever been sent down is to describe a God who does not speak. The passage says that is a shrunken picture. Naming Moses then does the work of the argument. The Book he brought was acknowledged right across the region, and its existence answers the general denial without any appeal to the present case.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical phrase about not appraising God with the appraisal He is due.
Describes the same Book brought by Moses in the same terms, containing guidance and light.
Names the promise to make scripture clear to people and not to conceal any part of it.

studies.applyIt: Ask whether your working picture of God includes His speaking to people. Many of us hold the idea of a maker easily and the idea of being spoken to awkwardly. Read one page of the Quran today as something said rather than something written, aloud if you can. The difference is not soft. It is exactly what this passage says was being underrated.
studies.explainEasier: They did not think of God highly enough. They said God never sent anything down to any person. But God sent the Book that Moses brought, and it was light and guidance for people.

studies.title: The Mother Of Cities
studies.meaning: One sentence says four things about this Book at once. It was sent down, it is blessed, and it confirms what came before it. It also has a job to do: to warn one particular city and everything around it. Early scholars identify the Mother of Cities as Mecca, and they discuss how far around it the warning reaches. Answers run from the nearby settlements all the way to the whole earth. The words at the end name who responds, and they tie belief in the hereafter to a habit rather than to an opinion.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, and the phrase naming the city belongs to that setting. The surah is addressing the very place where it was being recited. The word for confirming what came before assumes an audience that knew about earlier scripture. The Meccans did, through trade and through the communities along their routes. No occasion is reported for this verse in the classical sources.

keyTerms.note: From a root for a camel kneeling and settling down, giving the idea of good that stays in place. Blessing in Arabic is plenty that has come to rest rather than a burst of it.
A phrase for the settlement that others come from, the way a mother is the origin of a family. It names Mecca by what it does rather than by size, since the place was not large.

An intensive form of the verb for preserving, from the same root that gives the word for the guardians mentioned earlier in this surah. Applied to prayer, it means keeping something rather than performing it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca was small, dry and poor as farmland. It mattered because of the sanctuary and the trade routes that met there. Settlements around it lived off the pilgrimage season and the caravans the city organised. Calling it the mother of cities described a real dependence the region knew about. It had nothing to do with the size of the place or its wealth.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase naming the city turns up only twice in the whole Quran, here and in a later Meccan surah. Both times it sits inside a sentence about warning. The other passage adds that the Quran was revealed in Arabic for exactly that purpose. The classical commentaries read the two together as a pair.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The Book is described as carrying on from what came before it, not as a replacement. That shapes how the earlier scriptures are to be regarded. Then the words at the end make a quieter point. Belief in the hereafter is tied to guarding the prayer. So a conviction about what comes later shows up as a practice now, and the practice is treated as the visible form of that belief rather than as its result.

crossReferences.why: Names the same city and the same purpose, warning it and those around it, in an Arabic recitation.
Describes the revelation with the same word for blessed, and asks whether they will deny it.
States the confirming relationship at length, as a measure over the scriptures that came before.

studies.applyIt: Notice whether your prayers are things you perform or things you keep. The verb here is about guarding something, the way you guard an appointment you would not miss. Pick the prayer most likely to slip this week and protect it in advance, by deciding now where you will be and what will be paused.
studies.explainEasier: This Book was sent down too, and it is blessed. It agrees with the books that came before it. It is there to warn the Mother of Cities and the places around it. People who believe in the next life believe in it and keep up their prayers.

studies.title: In The Floods Of Death
studies.meaning: The question about who does greater wrong comes back, and this time three answers are given. One is inventing a lie against God. One is claiming a revelation that never came. One is offering to produce something like what God sent down. Early scholars connect these to men who made such claims at the time, though their identifications differ. Then the scene shifts abruptly to a deathbed. Angels reach out and tell the soul to give itself up, and the reason arrives in the same breath: what was said about God, and pride before His signs.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, in a passage about who may speak for God. The claim to produce something comparable was made publicly in the city, and the Quran elsewhere records the challenge to try it. The classical sources name different individuals behind the two middle claims and do not agree with each other. So the verse is best read as describing a kind of claim rather than one particular man.

keyTerms.note: Water deep enough to cover a person completely, from a root for submerging. Death is described as a rising level rather than a blow, which matches how dying is usually experienced from inside.
The participle for spreading something open, used of an outstretched hand. Arabic uses the same gesture for giving and for taking, so the picture is direct without needing to be explained.
From a root for being light in weight and therefore of little account. The punishment is named by the loss of standing rather than by pain, which answers the pride mentioned at the end.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Drowning was the particular terror of a people who mostly could not swim and who crossed the Red Sea for trade. Flash floods in the valleys were more familiar still. A dry valley bed could fill in minutes after rain somewhere out of sight, and people camped in them died without warning. The word used here for death belongs to that experience of water arriving and rising.
studies.didYouKnow: The question that opens this verse, asking who does greater wrong, is the same question that opened an earlier verse in this surah. Reading the two together shows the later one expanding the earlier. What was a single clause about inventing against God becomes three separate claims about speaking in His name.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Speaking falsely for God is placed at the far end of wrongdoing. The reason given at the end pairs it with pride before the signs, and the two belong together. Claiming to speak for God and refusing what He has said are both ways of putting the self where revelation should be. The scene at death then removes the chance of going on, which is what makes it the natural place for the passage to end.

crossReferences.why: Opens with the identical question earlier in this surah, with one clause where this has three.
Gives a parallel scene of angels taking souls, described from outside rather than through the dying.
Records the answer to the third claim: an invitation to produce a single comparable chapter.

studies.applyIt: Notice how often you attach God's name to your own preferences in conversation, in phrases that make a personal view sound settled. Everybody does it, and mostly without noticing. Once today, catch yourself before the phrase and say the opinion as your own instead. It is a small correction, and this passage is about the direction it points in.
studies.explainEasier: The worst wrong is lying about God. It is also wrong to say a message came to you when none did, or to offer to make something like what God sent. At death the angels reach out and tell such people to hand over their souls.

studies.title: You Have Come Alone
studies.meaning: Three things are named as missing. The company is gone, because each person arrives singly, just as they were first created. The possessions are gone too, described as left behind your back, which early scholars note is where something sits when you walk away from it rather than when it is taken from you. And the go-betweens are gone, along with the claim that they had a share in you. The words at the end state the result as a cutting: whatever ran between you has been severed.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, in a society built entirely around belonging. A person in Arabia was a member of a group before being one person, protected by a clan and known by a family line. Wealth was held and shown off together. Saying that people arrive one by one removed every structure the audience leaned on to say who they were. That, more than any picture of torment, is what gives the scene its force.

keyTerms.note: A plural formed from the word for one, so the Arabic says many people each alone. It describes a crowd of individuals rather than solitude, which is a more precise and a stranger picture.
