It gives the food dispute a wider frame before that dispute is taken up.

keyTerms.note: What is visible on the surface, from the root for a back or an exterior. The word gives the Arabic for something obvious, and it is used across the Quran as one half of a standard pair.
The interior, from the root for a belly. Paired with the word before it, the two cover a thing completely, so naming both halves of wrongdoing leaves no part of it unaddressed.
The same verb used earlier in this surah for the gilded speech passed between enemies. Its return ties the argument about food to the mechanism described a few lines before.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Reputation was a full-time job in a city where everyone knew everyone. A man's outward conduct was watched constantly, and his standing depended on it. So the gap between what was seen and what was not could be wide. Naming both halves in one breath spoke to a society that had refined the handling of the visible half into an art.
studies.didYouKnow: The pairing of outward and inward here is the standard Arabic way of saying all of something. English does the same with inside and out. The Quran uses these two words elsewhere of blessings, of the sea and of knowledge. So the phrase places wrongdoing inside a familiar figure for wholeness.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Naming the hidden side makes character the subject rather than reputation, and it does that without a word about being watched. The passage then draws a line from a small argument about food to something much larger. Giving in to pressure in a matter framed as trivial is described as serious. What is at stake is not the matter but who is being followed. That is a claim about how loyalty actually shifts.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same pairing, naming what is apparent of immoralities and what is concealed of them.
Describes those who avoid the greater wrongs and forgive when they are angry, as a settled quality.
Notes that the ones who avoid the great sins are still known best by the One who formed them.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you do only when nobody can see. Then take one thing you do only because someone can. Write both down on the same piece of paper. You do not have to act on either today. This passage puts the two halves in one sentence, and seeing them side by side is most of the work.
studies.explainEasier: Leave sin alone, the kind people can see and the kind they cannot. Do not eat food that God's name was not said over. Bad voices push their friends to argue with you about it.

studies.title: A Light To Walk By
studies.meaning: Two figures are set against each other. One was dead, then given life and a light to walk by among people. The other is in darkness and cannot get out. Early scholars notice a detail in the first description. The light is for walking among people, not for seeing alone, so what was given shows up in company. The second figure is described without any verb of choosing. He is simply in it. And the words at the end explain why that state lasts.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, and the classical scholars discuss whether the comparison points at particular people in the city. Different names are offered. Others read it as describing two conditions in general. The reports do not agree, and the wording works either way. What is not in dispute is the setting. Some in the community had accepted the message and others had refused it, living in the same streets.

keyTerms.note: The causative of living, used through the Quran for reviving dead ground after rain. Applying it to a person makes the change a small resurrection rather than an improvement.
Left unspecified, so these words do not say what the light is. Early scholars offer faith, the Quran and understanding, and the tradition records the range without narrowing it.
An active participle in a negative construction, so what is denied is the person as an emerger rather than a single exit. The grammar makes the condition a description rather than an event.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Walking at night in a town without lighting meant carrying a flame, or knowing the ground by memory. A lamp changed everything. You saw the drop, the sleeping animal, the person coming the other way. Those without one waited for dawn, or felt their way along the walls. Everybody in that audience had done both, and knew which they preferred.
studies.didYouKnow: The light here is given for walking among people, not for seeing alone in the dark. The same phrase appears in a later surah, where believers walk with their light going before them. The Quran keeps attaching this image to movement in company rather than to private lighting.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The change described is not an improvement in someone's opinions. It is a restoration of life, which sets the stakes higher than persuasion. And the purpose of the light is social. What has been received becomes visible in how a person moves among others. So the difference between the two figures is meant to be noticeable rather than inward. The words at the end keep the second figure's state explained rather than merely condemned.

crossReferences.why: Describes God bringing believers out of darkness into light, and the reverse for those who refuse.
Shows the same light in motion, going before believers and to their right on that day.
Draws out the other half of the comparison at length, as darkness layered over darkness at sea.

studies.applyIt: Think of one person whose presence makes a room easier to be in. Try to name what they actually do. It is usually small and repeatable: they ask, they wait, they do not compete. This verse describes light as something you walk with among people, so it is visible in behaviour before it is anything else.
studies.explainEasier: Think of a man who was dead. God brought him back to life and gave him a light to walk with among people. He is not the same as a man stuck in the dark who cannot get out.

studies.title: The Greatest Of Its Criminals
studies.meaning: An observation is made about how towns are arranged. In each one the leading wrongdoers are also its most prominent men. Early scholars note the word order, which puts greatness first and crime second, so the phrase names people who are great in the town's own reckoning. Their activity is scheming. The correction comes at once, and it is the whole point. Whatever they plot lands on themselves, and they do not sense it. That makes the scheming self-directed without their knowing.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, and the description fitted the city exactly. The opposition there was led by men of standing, heads of clans with wealth, clients and reputations. Their objections carried weight because of who they were rather than what they said. The verse then widens that arrangement to every town, which removes any sense that Mecca was unusually bad.

keyTerms.note: A plural for those greatest in a place, by age, wealth or standing. Its position before the word for wrongdoers makes prominence the first thing said about them, which is how the town itself would describe them.
A verb for planning in secret, not necessarily for evil ends, though usually so in the Quran. It names indirect action, working through arrangements rather than through open force.
From the root for fine awareness, the same one behind the word for a poet. Denying it says the effect is real and below the threshold of their noticing, not that they are indifferent to it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca's power sat with a handful of families. They held the offices of the sanctuary and financed the caravans, and they could make or break a man by withdrawing protection. They met, discussed and acted together, with no formal body existing at all. The word for scheming describes exactly that. A few people decided things in private, and everyone else met the result as circumstances.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran uses the verb for scheming of God as well, in passages where a plot is answered in kind. The classical scholars discuss that usage carefully. The word itself carries no moral charge in Arabic. It names planning that is concealed, and the surrounding sentence supplies the judgement.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage says that harm arranged against others comes back to the people who arranged it. That is how things work, not an occasional punishment. It is a claim about a moral order built into events rather than laid over them. The detail about not sensing it is what makes the verse unsettling. The mechanism runs whether or not anyone notices, so a person can be well into their own ruin and still be reading the situation as success.

crossReferences.why: States the principle directly, that an evil plot encircles none but the people who made it.
Names the same class of people, the affluent of a town, as the ones whose conduct decides its fate.
Shows the two sides afterwards, the followers and the ones they followed, arguing about who misled whom.

studies.applyIt: Think about a small arrangement you have made at work or at home that quietly disadvantages someone. You would not describe it out loud in those terms, and most of us have one. Say it plainly to yourself. The warning here is not about being caught. It is about a cost that arrives without being noticed.
studies.explainEasier: In every town God has let the biggest wrongdoers become its leading men, so they can scheme there. But their scheming only comes back on them. They do not even notice it.

studies.title: God Knows Where To Place It
studies.meaning: The objection is finally stated in full, and it is about status. They will not believe until they are given what God's messengers were given. That is a demand to be selected rather than addressed. The answer is a single clause. God knows best where He places His message. Early scholars note that it does not argue about their qualifications. It moves the question, since placing is the sender's decision, and no candidate is in a position to judge it.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, and the complaint had a concrete form. The classical sources record leading men of the city asking why the message had not come to someone of greater standing. They meant someone in Mecca, or in the town to the east. The Quran preserves that objection elsewhere in almost those words. The claim rested on wealth and clan, which were the city's only measures of importance.

keyTerms.note: A noun for what is sent with a messenger, distinct from the messenger himself. The word treats prophethood as a consignment placed somewhere, which is what makes the verb for placing exact.
From the root for being small in size. It names the loss of standing rather than pain, which answers exactly what the objectors were asking for, since their demand was about being large.
The comparative of knowing joined to a word for place. The construction is unusual and puts the weight on location, so what God knows best is the where of it, not the who.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Honour in Mecca was measured and displayed. Precedence at a gathering was counted publicly, and so was the right to speak first, the size of a man's following, and the number of guests he could feed. Being passed over for a distinction was a real injury, with money attached. In that world, the demand recorded here was a perfectly ordinary complaint about protocol.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for humiliation at the end of this verse appears only once in the whole Quran. It comes from the ordinary root for smallness. Its rarity marks a precise answer. The punishment named for men who demanded greatness is described by the word for being made small.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Selection is placed outside every visible qualification, which unsettles both the powerful and anyone who ranks themselves. The clause about knowing where to place the message says nothing about merit. It speaks only about the sender's judgement. That closes off two errors at once. One is resenting who was chosen. The other is assuming that being chosen shows anything a person could have arranged.

crossReferences.why: Preserves the complaint in its plainest form, asking why it did not come to a great man of two cities.
States the principle broadly: your Lord creates and chooses, and the choice is not theirs.
Records a related demand, that each of them be handed scrolls of his own, spread open.

studies.applyIt: Think of a time you were passed over and someone else was chosen. Notice whether you concluded anything about your own worth from it, because most of us do. Sit with the possibility that selection tracks something you cannot see, in either direction. That is not consolation. It is a more accurate account of what happened.
studies.explainEasier: When a sign comes, they say they will not believe unless they get what God's messengers got. God knows best where to put His message. Shame and hard punishment are waiting for those who scheme.

studies.title: As If Climbing The Sky
studies.meaning: Two states are described in physical terms. One chest is opened wide for submission. The other is made narrow and tight. Then a comparison arrives that has struck readers in every century: as though he were climbing into the sky. Early scholars explain it as the breathlessness of climbing beyond where air will hold you. That is a remarkably exact description of an experience nobody in that century could have had. What is named is not resistance but tightness.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, and the passage answers why some accept and some do not after every argument has been made. The surah has offered signs from creation, from history, and from the shape of revelation itself. This verse steps behind all of that. It describes the receiving state directly, in a city where both responses were on display inside the same families.

keyTerms.note: A verb for laying something open, used of cutting meat flat to dry. The same word titles a short surah addressed to the Prophet about his own chest being opened.
Read in two ways by the early authorities, giving either extreme narrowness or a thicket so dense nothing can enter. Both readings survive in the commentaries, and both describe blocked passage.
An intensive form built for difficulty, so the climb is laboured rather than smooth. The doubling of letters in the Arabic does the work a whole English phrase about struggling would need.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The Arabs knew height from mountains, not from anything higher. Climbing the peaks around Mecca, or in the highlands to the south, left a person short of breath. The chest works harder for less, and shepherds knew that feeling. So did anyone who had walked up out of a valley in the heat. That is the experience the comparison starts from.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for opening the chest here is the same one used at the start of a short late-Meccan surah. That surah is addressed to the Prophet, and it asks whether his own chest was not opened for him. So the same image describes what happened to him and what happens to anyone guided.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Guidance is described as a change in capacity rather than in argument. That explains why the surah's long case has convinced some and not others. Something has to be open for anything to enter. The passage gives both states to God's will, while the whole surah holds people responsible. The mainstream tradition keeps both without collapsing them, treating the tightness as following refusal rather than causing it.

crossReferences.why: Asks about the one whose chest God has opened to submission, so that he stands on a light.
Turns the same image into a prayer, where Moses asks for his own chest to be opened.
Opens a short surah with the same verb, asking whether the chest was not laid open already.

studies.applyIt: Notice where in your body you feel resistance when something true and unwelcome is said to you. For most people it is the chest or the throat, and it arrives before any thought does. Name it once when it happens today. This verse describes belief and refusal as physical states, and the physical part is the one you can catch.
studies.explainEasier: When God wants to guide someone, He opens up his chest. When He leaves someone to go astray, He makes his chest tight and narrow. It feels like climbing high up into the sky.

studies.title: The Home Of Peace
studies.meaning: The path just described is named as the Lord's own, and straight. The detailed explanation is said to be for people who take a reminder. Then the destination is given a name rather than a description. It is the Home of Peace, held with their Lord. Early scholars note that the word covers safety, wholeness and greeting all at once. The words at the end make God their protector, and they attach that relationship to what they used to do, not to a status they were handed.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, and this pair closes the surah's long argument before it turns to particular customs. The audience had been offered warnings for many verses. The naming of a destination here is one of the surah's few extended notes of promise. No occasion is reported. The word for peace also worked as the ordinary Arabian greeting, which gave the name an everyday warmth.

keyTerms.note: The first word means a dwelling with a courtyard, a family compound rather than a house. The second covers safety, soundness and the greeting itself, so the name promises a settled place free of harm.
A form of remembering that means retrieving what is already held. The audience for the detailed explanation is defined by a capacity for recollection rather than by any prior belief.
The relationship the surah has denied to every other candidate, now affirmed. In Arabian usage it named the person who stood behind you, which makes the promise social rather than only spiritual.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A home in Arabia meant a walled compound with a courtyard, animals, and several families inside it. It was where a traveller finally stopped. Safety there was taken for granted, and the greeting of peace was said at the gate. Naming the end point with that word promised the relief of arriving somewhere you no longer have to watch the road.
studies.didYouKnow: The name given here for the final destination appears twice in the Quran, and both times in a Meccan surah. Both times people are invited to it rather than described as living in it. The word for peace inside it is also one of the names by which God is described elsewhere.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The destination is named by its quality rather than pictured, which is unusual in a book with vivid pictures on hand. What is promised first is peace, and only then anything else. The words at the end are careful in a way worth noticing. God is their protector because of what they used to do. So the bond is tied to a life, not declared over a class of people.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same name for the destination, saying God invites to the Home of Peace generally.
Gives the greeting spoken at arrival, peace upon you for the patience you kept.
Names the same straight path as a daily request rather than as a description of a group.

studies.applyIt: Say the greeting of peace to one person today whom you would normally pass without speaking. It could be a neighbour, a colleague on another floor, someone at a counter. The word here names a home at the end of the road. It is also just a polite hello. Saying it on purpose once makes the link audible.
studies.explainEasier: This is your Lord's straight path. The signs are spelled out for people who pay attention. For them there is a Home of Peace with their Lord, and He is their protector because of what they did.

studies.title: We Profited From Each Other
studies.meaning: A gathering is described. Unseen beings are addressed for having taken many humans, and it is their human partners who answer. The answer is unusually frank. We took our enjoyment of one another, and we reached the term You appointed. Early scholars note that no defence is offered. The relationship is described as mutual benefit, which is exactly what it was. The reply that follows names the outcome, with an exception attached that the tradition discusses without settling.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, and the arrangement being described was a working part of Arabian religion. Travellers sought protection from the unseen powers of a place. Men consulted diviners who claimed such contacts, and got guidance and standing in return. Both sides gained something concrete. The verse does not caricature the relationship, and it lets one party describe it accurately.

keyTerms.note: A form meaning to seek or acquire a great deal of something. Applied to human beings it treats them as a quantity gathered, which is this verse's judgement on the relationship in a single word.
A verb for drawing use and pleasure from something, the root behind the word for goods and provisions. It names an exchange of advantage, which is how the speakers themselves describe what happened.
From a verb meaning to stay somewhere for a long time. It names a residence rather than a punishment, which makes the sentence a statement of where they now live.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian travellers entering a strange valley would seek the protection of its resident power, and they did this before making camp. Diviners in the settlements claimed ties with such beings, which made them consulted and paid. Both arrangements delivered something. One gave a sense of safety on the road, and the other gave a living at home. The exchange described here was a known feature of ordinary life.
studies.didYouKnow: The reply here contains an exception: that they remain except as God wills. The classical scholars discuss its scope at length without reaching agreement. It is one of the passages where the tradition openly records that the limit of a statement is not settled. The commentaries preserve the range of readings.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage lets a corrupt deal be described in its own terms, and the description condemns it without help. Nobody claims to have been tricked; they say they profited. That puts the fault in the exchange itself rather than in a mistake. And it names a pattern that outlasts the practice: deals in which two sides gain and something else is spent quietly between them.

crossReferences.why: Shows the other side of the same scene, with the beings themselves disowning those who worshipped them.
Describes the practice as it operated, men seeking refuge in unseen beings and increasing their burden.
Records a similar speech afterwards, in which the tempter admits he had no power beyond an invitation.

studies.applyIt: Think of an arrangement in your life where two people each get something and neither would describe it out loud. A friendship of mutual flattery, or a work relationship built on cover. Name what each of you is actually collecting. That is the whole exercise here. The naming is uncomfortable, and that is usually because it is accurate.
studies.explainEasier: On that day God will gather everyone. The unseen beings and the people who followed them will admit that each side got something out of the other. Now their time is up.

studies.title: Wrongdoers Made Allies
studies.meaning: One short line states a principle about how alliances form. Some wrongdoers are made close to others, and the reason given is what they used to earn. Early scholars read this as a natural sorting rather than an imposed punishment. Conduct draws like conduct, and people end up among those whose habits match their own. The verb used is the one for making someone a patron or ally, so what is described is not merely company. It is the protective bond Arabia was built on.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, and this follows a scene where two parties admit openly that each gained. The surah has been describing an opposition that acted together. This verse explains how such groups form. No occasion is reported. The point would have been instantly clear in a city where alliances between families shifted with shared interest.

keyTerms.gloss: We make allies, set as patrons
keyTerms.note: From the root for nearness that gives the word for a protector, used through this surah. It describes assigning one party to another as an ally, not merely letting them associate.
From a root meaning to put something out of its place. Wrongdoing in Arabic is misplacement, which fits a line about people ending up in the company their conduct has sorted them into.
The commercial verb used at the opening of this surah for what God knows of a person. Its return here makes the alliance a return on conduct rather than an accident of circumstance.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Alliances were formal and sworn. Two clans would bind themselves to defend each other, and such pacts were remembered for generations and recited in poetry. Choosing an ally was the weightiest decision a family made, and it was made on shared interest. Everyone understood that you ended up beside people whose way of working matched your own.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb here shares its root with the word for a protector, and the surah has been using that word since its early pages. There it asks whether any protector besides God should be taken. So the same three letters mark two things at once. They mark the relationship that is denied and the one that forms by default.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Company is presented as a consequence rather than a choice made fresh each time. What a person does draws them toward others doing the same. The passage gives that sorting to God while tying it plainly to conduct. The result is a claim worth taking seriously. The circle you find yourself in is information about you. It built up by a process you were part of without deciding.

crossReferences.why: States the same sorting from both sides, with wrongdoers as allies and God as ally of the mindful.
Describes those who refuse as allies of one another, and warns what follows if that is not answered.
Shows what becomes of such alliances afterwards, when close friends turn into enemies.

studies.applyIt: Look at the five people you spend most time with. Ask what habit you all share that none of you would defend. Not the good things, which are easy to see. This verse says company forms around conduct, so the shared habit is usually the invisible reason the group works.
studies.explainEasier: In this way God lets people who do wrong become friends and helpers to each other. It happens because of the kind of things they keep doing.

studies.title: Messengers From Among You
studies.meaning: The question put at the gathering is procedural. Did messengers not come to you, from among yourselves, relating My signs and warning of this meeting. The phrase from among you carries the weight, since a messenger of your own kind removes the excuse of not understanding. The answer is a confession rather than a defence. The verse adds the explanation without being asked: the life of this world deceived them. Then the confession is repeated, in the narrator's voice.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, and the objection answered here has run through the surah from its opening pages. That objection was that a human messenger was not enough. This verse puts it in the past tense and shows it withdrawn by the people who raised it. The classical scholars discuss the address to both kinds of being, and their readings of how messengers reached the unseen ones vary.

keyTerms.note: Two words that answer the surah's longest-running objection. A messenger of your own kind can be understood and copied, which is the argument the earlier verses made about angels at some length.
From the root for following a track, which gives the word for a story. Relating something is described as following its trail, so a narrative is a set of footprints rather than an invention.
The legal verb for giving testimony, used here of the accused testifying against themselves. It turns the scene into a hearing where the only witness called is the defendant.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A proper hearing in Arabia began by establishing that the parties had been informed. A claim could not proceed if a man had never been told of the duty. Elders would ask first whether notice had been given. The form of the question here follows that procedure exactly. An audience used to arbitration would have recognised the opening move.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used for the messengers relating the signs comes from the root that gives the Quran its word for a story. The same root produces the verb for tracking an animal by its prints. Narrating and tracing a trail are one action in Arabic. That is why a Quranic story is presented as something followed rather than composed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets out that nobody is answerable for what they were never told, and it does so by having the parties confirm it themselves. That makes the whole scene procedural rather than vengeful. The explanation slipped in between the two confessions is the most humane touch. They were deceived by the present life. That is offered not as an excuse but as an accurate account of what happened to them.

crossReferences.why: States the principle plainly, that punishment does not come until a messenger has been sent.
Puts the identical question at the gate, and records the same admission that warners did come.
Gives the fullest version of the exchange, including the answer that a warner came and was denied.

studies.applyIt: Think of a warning you have already received more than once, about your health, your work, or a relationship. Not a vague worry, but an actual warning from someone. Write down what it was in one sentence. This verse turns on whether notice was given. Most of the notices we are given are forgotten rather than refused.
studies.explainEasier: God asks whether messengers from their own kind did not come to them, telling them His signs and warning about this day. They admit that it is true. Life in this world had fooled them.

studies.title: Never While They Were Unaware
studies.meaning: The first of these two lines gives the reason for the hearing just described. Towns are not destroyed for wrongdoing while their people are unaware, so notice comes before consequence, as a matter of principle. Early scholars read the unawareness as covering those who never received a message at all. Then the second line refuses a single verdict for everyone. Each has degrees according to what they did. So the outcome is graded rather than sorted into two piles, and nothing anyone did has gone unnoticed.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, closing a sequence about the questioning at the gathering. The surah has spent many verses on peoples destroyed before. This passage supplies the standard those accounts assume. The Meccans travelled past ruined settlements twice a year, and had been asked repeatedly to consider them. Here they are told what condition every one of those cases met first.

keyTerms.note: From a root for being inattentive to something present. It covers both never having been told and having been told and not attending, and the closing words deny the same quality of God.
Steps of a stair, the same word used earlier in this surah for the raising of Abraham. Its use here for everyone makes the final accounting continuous rather than divided into two categories.
Read by early scholars in two ways: destroying them for their wrongdoing, or destroying them unjustly. Both readings are old, and each yields a different emphasis in the same sentence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arab law worked by warning. A tribe planning to act against another gave formal notice, and treaties were torn up in the open before fighting began. Striking without that step was itself a disgrace, and poetry records the shame of the surprise raid. People raised on those customs would hear this as a rule they already took as the mark of honest dealing.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for heedlessness in the first line returns at the end of the second. There it is applied to God in the negative. So the same term does two jobs. It describes the condition that protects people from judgement, and the condition God never occupies. The Arabic makes that symmetry visible, and translations usually lose it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two principles are stated together, and each limits the other. Nobody is held to what they were never given. Everybody is held to what they did, in degrees. The result is a picture of answering for your life that is neither sweeping nor soft. The words at the end also remove the idea that small acts fall below the threshold of notice. That is where most of a life actually happens.

crossReferences.why: States the same rule for earlier towns, that none was destroyed without warners sent as a reminder.
Applies the principle to a mother city, where a messenger is sent before anything is decided.
Repeats the grading of outcomes by what each person did, so that nobody is treated as a category.

studies.applyIt: Notice a rule you enforce at home or at work that people around you have never actually been told. It might be about tidiness, timing, or tone. Say it out loud once this week, before you next hold anyone to it. These lines make notice the condition of fairness, and the same standard is cheap to apply.
studies.explainEasier: Your Lord does not wipe out a town for its wrongdoing while its people have not been warned. Everyone gets a place that fits what they did. Your Lord is never unaware of what people do.

studies.title: Rich Beyond Need, Owner Of Mercy
studies.meaning: Two descriptions are placed side by side, and early scholars note that the pairing does the work. God is free of all need, so nothing is owed to anyone. And He is the owner of mercy, which is why the situation is not what independence alone would produce. What follows is a statement of capacity. He could remove you and put others in your place. That is exactly how you were raised from the descendants of another people. The words that close it promise something that cannot be dodged.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, and the reminder about descent from another people had an edge to it. The city traced its standing through ancestry. Meccan families held their position by lineage and by inherited offices. The surah has already argued that guidance does not travel that way. Here even their existence as a people is described as a succession that replaced someone else.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to be self-sufficient, which also gives the word for wealth. Applied to God it denies need rather than asserting possession, which is why mercy has to be named separately.
From the root for coming after someone, which gives the word for a successor. It names replacement in an office or a place, so the sentence is about position rather than about destruction.
From a root for weakness and inability, in a form meaning to make someone unable. The denial says nothing anyone does can make the promise fail, which is a claim about capacity, not about effort.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia's past was a story of one people taking the place of another. Tribes pushed tribes off wells and pastures. The ruins along the trade roads belonged to peoples whose names survived only in poetry. Mecca's own leading tribe had taken charge of the sanctuary from an earlier group, within living memory. Nobody there needed persuading that one people could follow another.
studies.didYouKnow: The two descriptions opening this passage, free of need and owner of mercy, appear together in this exact pairing only here in the Quran. Each is common on its own. Placed side by side they answer a question the surah has raised repeatedly. Why is anything at all given to people who have nothing to offer.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Independence and mercy are held together, and neither alone would produce what the passage describes. A God who needed something could be bargained with. A God free of need but without mercy would have no reason to send anything. The reminder about succession then removes any sense of entitlement to a place in the world. And the promise that follows removes the hope of outlasting the account.

crossReferences.why: States the same two ideas: you are the needy ones, and He could remove you and bring a new creation.
Repeats the capacity for replacement plainly, that He could take you away and bring others.
Says the same thing about creation as a whole, and calls it no great matter for God.

studies.applyIt: Think of a role you hold that will one day belong to someone else: a job, a place in a family, a duty in a community. Picture the person who will hold it after you, without gloom. Then ask what you would want them to inherit from how you are doing it. That question usually clears things up within a minute.
studies.explainEasier: Your Lord needs nothing from anyone, and mercy belongs to Him. If He wanted, He could take you away and put other people in your place. What you are promised is coming, and you cannot stop it.

studies.title: Work, And So Will I
studies.meaning: The instruction sounds almost like a truce, and it is not one. Each side is told to work according to its position, and the speaker says that he is working too. What settles the matter is put off to knowledge that will arrive, not to argument now. You will come to know whose is the outcome of the abode. Early scholars note the confidence in the words at the end. They state plainly that wrongdoers do not come out ahead, so the delay is about timing rather than doubt.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, and this formula appears in several surahs from the same period. It is always addressed to a community that had run out of arguments to make. It belongs to the stage where persuasion had been tried at length and was being set down. The classical sources record no specific occasion. The repetition across surahs suggests a standing posture rather than a single moment.

keyTerms.note: A noun of place, covering both where a person stands and the standing they have. The word lets the instruction mean work in your own way and according to what you actually are.
From the root for a heel and for following behind, so an outcome is what comes after a thing has passed. The surah used it earlier when telling listeners to travel and see how peoples ended.
From a root meaning to split open ground for planting, which gives the word for a farmer. Success in Arabic is a harvest reached, so failure here means never arriving at what was worked for.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Farming in an oasis was a long wager. Ground was cleared, water rights secured and palms planted years before anything came back. Nobody claimed a result until the harvest was in the store. The word for success here belongs to that world, which is why the answer offered is not an argument but an invitation to wait for the crop.
studies.didYouKnow: This exact instruction appears in three separate places in the Quran. It tells opponents to work in their own way while the speaker works in his. Each place is a different surah, and each is spoken by a messenger to his own people. The repetition marks it as the standard closing move when persuasion has run out.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage models disagreement that has stopped pretending talk will resolve it, and it does so without hostility. Both sides are told to act, which treats the opponent as a serious agent rather than an obstacle. The appeal is to an outcome rather than to an argument. That places the matter under time, where it can actually be settled. The last line makes clear that the speaker is not neutral about which way it will go.

crossReferences.why: Puts the identical instruction in the mouth of an earlier prophet addressing his own community.
Repeats the same formula in another Meccan surah, followed by a promise that they will know.
Describes whose the final home is: those who seek no superiority on earth and cause no corruption.

studies.applyIt: Pick an argument you have been having in your head with someone who is not going to agree. Stop making the case. Instead, spend one hour this week doing the thing you have been trying to justify. The move here is to answer a dispute with work, and it is usually the only answer that lands.
studies.explainEasier: Keep working in your own way, and I will keep working in mine. You will find out in the end who gets the better home. People who do wrong never come out on top.

studies.title: This Share Is For God
studies.meaning: A custom is described with unusual precision. Produce and livestock were divided in two. One portion went to God and one to the objects worshipped beside Him. Then the accounting is exposed. What was set aside for the partners never reached God, while what was set aside for God found its way to them. Early scholars explain that shortfalls were made up in one direction only. The judgement that closes it is brief, and it is about the arithmetic rather than the theology.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, and the practice was real and locally recorded. Arabian communities set aside a share of harvest and herds for religious use, split between the high God and the shrine deities. The produce fed guests, custodians and the poor. The surah's closing section turns from argument to these inherited customs, describing several of them before answering.

keyTerms.note: A verb for scattering and multiplying, used of God producing creatures in abundance. Placing it in the sentence reminds the audience whose the crops and herds were before any division was made.
Land that has been ploughed and what grows on it, from the root for tilling. Paired with livestock it covers the two forms of wealth a farming society had, so the custom touched everything.

The same phrase used earlier in this surah for assertions made without support. Inserted in the middle of the sentence, it marks the words this is for God as their claim rather than a statement of fact.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Sharing out a harvest was public and watched. A family separated portions on the threshing floor while neighbours saw it done. The shares had names and set sizes, and livestock were divided the same way at certain seasons. Because everyone could see the piles, any quiet change between them was a social act as much as a religious one, and people knew who did it.
studies.didYouKnow: This verse preserves an unusually specific piece of pre-Islamic religious practice. It describes a division of produce that other sources also record. The surah's closing section works almost as a catalogue of such customs, naming four or five distinct ones in a few verses. It is one of the earliest written sources for them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The complaint is not that they gave. It is that the giving was quietly arranged to favour the recipient who could be seen. Everything named was created and provided in the first place, which makes the division a matter of returning rather than donating. The principle reaches past the specific custom. Any portion set aside for God that is later found useful for something else was never really set aside.

crossReferences.why: Records the same practice, assigning a portion of what was provided to what they do not even know.
Asks about provision that people have themselves divided into permitted and forbidden portions.
Addresses the same instinct in giving, not selecting the poorer part to give away.

studies.applyIt: Look at what you set aside for good purposes. Check whether any of it quietly comes back to you: a donation that buys standing, help offered where it will be noticed. You do not have to stop. Just find out which portion is actually leaving your hands. That is what this verse is measuring.
studies.explainEasier: They took part of their crops and animals. This share is for God, they said, and this share is for our idols. But the idols' share never reached God. God's share always ended up with the idols.

studies.title: Made To Seem Right
studies.meaning: The gravest of these customs is named, the killing of children, and the verse is careful about how it happened. It was made to look right to them, so the practice arrived dressed as duty rather than as cruelty. Two purposes are given for that dressing. One is to ruin them. The other is to confuse their religion until they could no longer tell what belonged to it. Early scholars note the sentence about God's will, which denies that the practice was beyond preventing. Then comes the instruction to leave them to their inventions.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, and the practice was real in parts of Arabia. The classical sources differ on how widespread it was. Motives recorded include fear of poverty and shame at the birth of daughters. The Quran addresses it in several surahs from this period and always names it directly, without softening. That is itself a comment on how it was normally discussed.

keyTerms.note: The same verb the surah uses for conduct dressed up until it looks acceptable. Its appearance here explains how something monstrous was carried out by ordinary people who believed themselves in the right.
From a root meaning to fall into a pit or perish. It names destruction by falling rather than by being struck, which suits a practice adopted step by step and defended each time.
From the root for clothing, so confusion is something laid over a thing. The surah has used the same verb twice already, of confusion put over a question and over a community.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Life at the edge of survival made every extra mouth a calculation. Drought years forced households into decisions they would not otherwise face. Daughters also carried the risk of capture in a raid, which brought a family lasting shame. None of this excuses anything. It explains how a custom could be defended by people who thought of themselves as responsible.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran returns to this practice in several passages, and each time it attacks the reasoning rather than only the act. It names the fear of poverty in one place and the shame at a daughter's birth in another. One late Meccan surah puts the question to the child directly, asking for what offence she was killed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage names the mechanism by which people do terrible things. The thing is presented to them as right. That is a more useful account than calling it wickedness, because it can be checked from the inside. It also names the second damage. Once such a practice is folded into religion, the religion itself becomes unreadable, and people lose the ability to tell what it actually asks of them.

crossReferences.why: Addresses the stated motive directly, answering fear of poverty with who provides for whom.
Describes the shame at a daughter's birth and the decision made in secret from the community.
Puts the question to the child herself on that day, asking for what sin she was killed.

studies.applyIt: Notice something your own society finds normal that you suspect will be looked back on with horror. Say what it is, even if only to yourself. Notice how quickly the justifications arrive. That arrival is the mechanism this verse names, and catching it working in your own reasoning is the point of the exercise.
studies.explainEasier: Their idols made killing their own children look like the right thing to do. It ruined them and it muddled their religion. God could have stopped it, so leave them to what they make up.

studies.title: Reserved For Whom We Please
studies.meaning: People in Mecca had carved up their own food supply and said God had drawn the lines. Certain livestock and crops were restricted, open only to those the owners named. Some animals had their backs put off limits, so nobody rode them. Over others no name of God was spoken. Early scholars explain each as a vow made after an animal bore so many young, or after a journey ended safely. Twice the verse slips the truth in: this is by their claims, an invention against God. The rules were real. Their source was not.
studies.historicalContext: This comes late in a Meccan surah, among customs the Arabs had inherited and never questioned. The animals named here appear elsewhere in the Quran under their Arabic names, and other early sources describe them too. Setting one aside was costly. A dedicated animal was never worked and never sold, so a household gave up real wealth, and neighbours counted that as piety. Just before this, the surah described a harvest being divided the same way.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to prevent or enclose, which gives the word for a lap and for a stone enclosure. The term names a barrier put around something rather than a quality the thing has.
The plural of back, naming what was placed off limits. An animal that could not be ridden or loaded was a household's wealth taken permanently out of use, which is what made the vow costly.
The verbal noun from the root used through this surah for fabricating. Placed at the end as a summary, it names the whole set of customs by what they have in common rather than one by one.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Picture a camel walking loose through a settlement that everyone has agreed to leave alone. It grazes where it likes. Nobody milks it for the family pot and nobody loads it, because a vow took it out of use for good. Everyone in the camp knows which animal it is, so the cost is as visible as the piety. That is part of why the practice held. The verse answers with three words: it was all by their claims.
studies.didYouKnow: A later verse given in Medina names four of these dedicated animal classes by their Arabic terms. It says flatly that God appointed none of them. Read the two passages together and something odd shows up. The Quran keeps a fairly close record of the old Arabian customs, and no other source writes them down in this much detail.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Here is the uncomfortable part. The people in this verse were sincere, their piety cost them real money, and none of that made the rule true. God puts one question to the whole arrangement: where did the requirement come from. Sacrifice never turns a practice into a command. That standard cuts both ways, weighing on the limits a person sets for himself as heavily as on the ones he sets for others. Naming the whole thing an invention against God places it beside the gravest charge in the surah.

crossReferences.why: Names four of these dedicated animal classes outright and denies that God appointed any of them.
Asks who gave permission to split provision into what is allowed and what is held back.
Warns against tongues that call things lawful or unlawful, inventing about God.

studies.applyIt: Think of one discipline you keep that costs you something and that you quietly count as a mark of seriousness. Ask where it came from. If it was your own good idea, keep it and call it that. This verse is not against costly practices. It is against the small upgrade from my practice to God's requirement.
studies.explainEasier: They said some animals and crops were off limits, and only the people they chose could eat them. They said other animals must never be ridden. Over some they never said God's name. They made all this up.

studies.title: Reserved For Our Males
studies.meaning: This was a rule about who eats when an animal gives birth. What is in the wombs of these animals, they said, is for our men and forbidden to our wives. Then comes the line that gives the whole thing away: if the young is born dead, everyone may share. Early scholars note how exactly the verse records that exception. A rule announced as a limit God set sends the valuable portion one way and the worthless portion to everybody. That is a division, not a restriction.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, near the end of a surah that has been walking through the customs people were born into. Arabian food rules often ran along lines of sex and rank, and they were kept as duties owed to God rather than as household preferences. The Quran answers them by repeating them in the speakers' own words and letting the arrangement show itself. This custom it records more precisely than the others.

keyTerms.note: From the root for something unmixed, which also gives the word for sincerity. Its use for a portion reserved to one group makes the claim of purity sit oddly beside what the rest of the ayah reports.
The plural of a word meaning one of a pair, used for husband and wife alike. Its presence names exactly who was excluded, so the arrangement cannot be described in neutral terms.
A verbal noun for characterising something in a certain way. What will be repaid is named as the describing itself, so the fault is located in the act of labelling rather than only in the practice.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: When meat was divided at a household it was divided by rank, and everyone standing there could see who received which cut. Women often ate after the men, from what was left. On a margin that thin those shares mattered for health and not only for pride. A rule that kept the best portion for one group had effects everybody in the compound could feel. What the verse repays them for is the claiming.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this verse uses for the portion reserved to the men comes from a surprising root. The same three letters give the Quran its word for sincerity, and its word for worship offered to God alone. So one root names undivided devotion and, in this line, a claim of exclusive right to a piece of meat.
studies.theologicalSignificance: This verse hands the reader a test rather than only a verdict. When a rule said to come from God keeps paying the people who announce it, that pattern is itself evidence about where the rule came from. No training is needed to run the test. It was given to an audience who could check it against their own cooking fires that same evening. And what God says He will repay them for is the describing itself, not only the meal.

crossReferences.why: Runs the same test on another claim, calling a division that favours the one dividing an unfair share.
Records the same lopsidedness, assigning to God what the speakers did not want for themselves.
Corrects the assumption underneath it, since God gives daughters and sons as He wills.

studies.applyIt: Look at a rule in your home or your workplace that you helped write, and ask who it favours on the days it is inconvenient. Not who it was meant to favour. If the answer keeps coming back to you, that is worth knowing. The test in this verse is simple arithmetic, and it works without anyone being accused of anything.
studies.explainEasier: They said the young inside these animals belonged only to their men, and their wives could not have any. But if it was born dead, then everyone could share it.

studies.title: They Forbade What Was Given
studies.meaning: The verdict on the whole run of customs lands here, and it puts two unlike things in one sentence. Killing your own children and declaring God's provision off limits are both called loss. Both are traced to one root, which is acting with no knowledge and inventing about God. Early scholars point to the word chosen for the folly, which means lightness of mind rather than cruelty. What these people lost was not property. It was themselves. The verse then says the outcome twice over, that they went astray and were not guided.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, at the close of the surah's walk through inherited custom. Nobody who kept these two practices thought of them as related. One was a hard economic decision made in a bad year, and the other was piety. The surah sets them side by side because both rested on a claim about what God had arranged, made by people who had been told nothing on the subject. No occasion is reported for this verse.

keyTerms.note: From a root for lightness and instability, used of a garment flapping loosely. It names a mind without weight rather than a wicked one, which is a specific and less comfortable accusation.

The verb behind the Quranic word for provision, covering food, livelihood and anything that sustains. Its presence makes the restriction a refusal of something already given rather than an act of restraint.
The commercial verb for a deal ending in deficit, used at the opening of this surah of those who lost themselves. The particle before it marks the loss as accomplished rather than threatened.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Both practices grew out of the same fear, the fear of not having enough. One household sat down and worked out whether it could feed another mouth. Another set aside an animal it was no longer allowed to use. Both were managing a margin so thin that one poor season could erase it, and both believed they were being responsible. Other passages answer that fear directly, by naming who actually provides for whom.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for folly here is the same one the Quran uses for people not competent to manage their own property. It also describes the one who turns away from the way of Abraham. What it names is a lack of weight in judgement. Early Arabic dictionary writers tie it to a rope or a garment that will not hold steady.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two practices at opposite ends of seriousness come from one failure, which is speaking for God without having been told anything. That shared root is what this surah keeps coming back to. Setting an unbearable act next to a merely mistaken one shows how far the damage from one error can reach. The verse also treats provision as something already handed over. So fencing it off is a refusal of a gift, not a choice to go without.

crossReferences.why: Asks plainly who forbade the good things of provision that God brought out for His servants.
Names the fear behind the first practice and answers it with who provides for parent and child alike.
Warns against banning the good things God made lawful, and against overstepping in either direction.

studies.applyIt: Notice one decision you are making mostly out of fear that there will not be enough. It might be a hesitation about hosting someone, or time you hold back. Name the fear instead of the reason you usually give. This verse traces two very different failures back to the same fear. The fear is easier to face than the choices built on top of it.
studies.explainEasier: They have lost everything. They kill their own children out of foolishness, with no real knowledge, and they ban the food God gave them. They made it up about God, and they have gone off the path.

studies.title: Give Its Due At Harvest
studies.meaning: After all the invented limits, the verse turns to what God actually asked, and it is three plain things. Eat of the fruit when it comes in. Give its due on the day you harvest it, and do not be excessive. Early scholars differ over what the due means here. Some read it as the required portion set out later, and others as the ordinary giving to the poor at harvest time. The tradition keeps both readings. The timing is the detail that catches you: on the day, before the crop has turned into something stored and owned.
studies.historicalContext: This came down in Mecca, years before the detailed arrangements for giving were laid out in Medina. That gap is why the scholars differ about how far the due reaches. The gardens in the verse, some trained up on trellises and some left to grow wild, belong to the oasis farming of the region. Mecca's own valley was bare. The verse answers the customs just described by saying what was really asked.

keyTerms.note: From the root for a structure raised up, used of vines trained over frames. Pairing it with untrellised covers cultivated and wild growth, so nothing that grows falls outside the sentence.
The word for a right owed rather than a favour offered. Calling the portion a due makes the recipient a claimant, which changes the posture of both giver and receiver.
From a root for going past a proper limit. Commentators apply it to both consumption and giving, since exceeding what is reasonable in generosity was also understood as a form of excess.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Harvest day in an oasis happened in the open. The dates were cut down, piled up and divided while neighbours and the poor of the settlement stood watching. The customary shares went out on the spot rather than being sent on later. Giving at that moment cost nothing extra in effort and everybody saw it. Once the crop went into the store room it belonged to the household in a different way, which is why the verse names the day of harvest.
studies.didYouKnow: The warning against excess here turns up almost word for word in another Meccan surah, where it is attached to eating and drinking instead of to a harvest. Both times it ends with the same words about what God does not love. Pairing a permission with a limit inside one sentence is a habit of these passages.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God gives permission to eat before He asks for anything, and the limit on waste comes after both. Enjoyment is not treated as suspicious here. What is asked is that a share be recognised as owed the moment the wealth arrives, before ownership has had time to settle. Calling that share a due rather than a gift removes the giver's advantage over the one receiving. The neighbour in need is a claimant here, not a beneficiary.

crossReferences.why: States the same principle about wealth in general, that a known share belongs to those in need.
Repeats the same words about excess almost exactly, applied there to eating and drinking.
Extends the warning about waste, calling the wasteful brothers of the devils.

studies.applyIt: The next time money arrives that you were not expecting, give a part of it away the same day rather than waiting until you have thought it over. The timing is the whole instruction. A sum that has sat in your account for a week starts to feel like yours. A sum that arrived this morning has not had the chance.
studies.explainEasier: God grows the gardens, the date palms, the crops, the olives and the pomegranates. Eat the fruit when it is ready, and give away its share on the day you pick it. Do not waste any of it.

studies.title: The Footsteps Of An Enemy
studies.meaning: The animals a family lived off are described by what they do. Some are big enough to carry loads, and some are kept for what they give closer to the ground. Early scholars differ over the exact sense of that second word. Then two instructions come. Eat of what God provided, which reopens everything the customs had closed off. And do not walk in the footsteps of the enemy. The image is exact: not his orders but his footprints, a path walked one step at a time by someone who never decided to take it.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, where the restrictions this surah is taking apart had piled up slowly. Nobody in the city woke up one morning and adopted the whole system. Each generation received it, kept it and added a little. Footsteps rather than orders describes that process precisely, which is why the image turns up here and not in a passage about open defiance.

keyTerms.note: From the verb for carrying, naming animals large enough to bear loads. It classifies livestock by function rather than by kind, which is how a herding household actually thought about them.
From the root for spreading something out, and read by commentators as smaller animals close to the ground, or as what their wool and hides are spread out to make. Both senses are preserved.
The plural of a single stride. Following footprints is different from obeying instructions, since each step is small, plausible and connected only to the one before it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Everyone could track. A herdsman reading prints in the sand knew which animal had passed, how long ago, and whether it was carrying a load. Children learned to follow a trail before they learned anything else. So following footsteps named something done confidently and half awake, eyes down, with no need to know where the trail ends. The verse borrows that walk for the enemy's path.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about following the footsteps of the enemy comes up four times in the Quran, and every one of them sits in a passage about ordinary conduct rather than grand wrongdoing. The subjects are food, wealth, gossip and how people treat each other. The image is saved for slow drift, not for dramatic rebellion.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Character is described as forming in steps rather than in decisions, and that is both a warning and a relief. Nobody chooses a whole direction at once, so nobody has to reverse one at once either. The instruction to eat what was provided matters here too. Undoing a restriction that had no warrant is treated as part of good conduct rather than as going soft. That keeps the passage from being read as a call for more caution.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same phrase, joining permission to eat what is good with the warning about footsteps.
Applies the same image to speech and reputation, where the first step looks entirely harmless.
Describes livestock by their benefits at greater length, including warmth, food and transport.

studies.applyIt: Think of a habit you would not have accepted three years ago, and trace the individual steps that brought you to it. There will be about five, and each one will have looked reasonable at the time. What this verse gives you is a trail rather than a decision. A trail can be walked back the way it was walked in.
studies.explainEasier: Some animals carry loads and some give wool and hides. Eat the food God has given you, and do not walk in the footsteps of Satan. He is a clear enemy to you.

studies.title: Eight Pairs Of Livestock
studies.meaning: The argument turns into a cross-examination. Eight pairs are counted out, beginning with sheep and goats. Then the question comes with no room left in it. Was it the two males that were withheld, or the two females, or what the females are carrying. Every possibility is named, so no answer can be made up on the spot. Early scholars note that the customs under challenge did not fall neatly into any of these boxes, which is exactly why the count is made. What is demanded at the end is knowledge, not an opinion.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, and the counting is deliberate. The restrictions people kept applied to certain animals in certain cases, arriving from vows and inherited practice rather than from any principle. So the whole herd is laid out as eight pairs, and then the question asks which group was actually named. That forces a general rule to be produced where only local custom existed.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word for one of a pair, so eight pairs means four kinds counted by male and female. The Quran uses the same word of human spouses and of created things generally.
From the root for a garment wrapped around the body. Applied to a womb it describes enclosure rather than possession, which keeps the third option in the question distinct from the first two.
An imperative from the root behind the words for weighty news and for a prophet. Demanding information in that form asks for something with a source behind it, not for a report of what people do.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The four animals named were the whole of a household's wealth. Sheep and goats gave milk, wool and meat, and were counted every day. Camels carried loads and crossed deserts, and cattle worked the land at the oases. A man's standing was stated in numbers of these. Dividing them into eight pairs is simply how anyone there would have taken stock.
studies.didYouKnow: The same eight pairs of livestock are counted again in another surah, and there they are listed among God's gifts rather than used in an argument. So one list does two jobs. Once it describes what was handed over, and once it frames a question about what was supposedly held back.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God asks that a claim about His requirements be stated as a general rule, in a form that can be looked at. The demand for knowledge at the end sets the bar. This is a way of testing rather than a doctrine, and it works wherever a practice hardens into an obligation. Listing creation in pairs does quiet work as well. The animals being argued over are shown first as things given.

crossReferences.why: Lists the same eight pairs among what was sent down for people, with no argument attached.
Names pairing as a feature of creation generally, among people and among the livestock alike.
Describes what these animals were given for, which the customs under dispute had partly cancelled.

studies.applyIt: Take a rule you have been told is required, and try to state it as a general principle in one sentence, without naming the case that prompted it. Some rules come through that intact and some do not. The method in this verse is exactly that translation. It usually takes about a minute to find out which kind you are holding.
studies.explainEasier: There are eight kinds of farm animals, counted as male and female. Ask them which ones God banned. Was it the two males, the two females, or the young inside the mothers. Tell me the truth, if you really know it.

studies.title: Were You There To Witness
studies.meaning: The same count is repeated for camels and cattle, and then a new question is added that goes past the rule to its source. Were you standing there when God charged you with this. Early scholars note that the demand has shifted from producing a rule to producing an occasion, and nobody could do that. The verse then names the wrongdoing outright, and adds something it had not said before. The invention is made in order to mislead people. That turns a private fault into one with victims.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, finishing the challenge begun a moment earlier. Religious authority in Arabia rested on inherited custom, and nobody ever claimed there had been a moment of instruction behind it. So the question about being present had no answer available. The surah knows that. It is asked to make the silence audible, not to collect a reply.

keyTerms.note: The word covers both being present at an event and testifying to it. The question uses the first sense to expose the absence of the second, since no one can testify to what they did not attend.
A verb for entrusting an instruction to someone, used for a solemn charge and for a will. The same verb returns a few ayat later, introducing what God actually did enjoin.
A purpose clause naming the effect of the invention on other people. It turns a private fabrication into an act with victims, which is why the ayah's judgement is stated in its strongest form.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Testimony in Arabia meant having been there. A man's word carried weight in proportion to whether he had seen the thing himself, and hearsay was known to be weaker even where nothing was written down. Asking whether someone was present when an instruction was given was a standard move in any dispute. Everybody in the audience knew what an evasive answer to it meant.
studies.didYouKnow: The question about being present when something was decreed comes up in a similar form in another surah, asked there of people who described the angels as female. Both times the challenge works the same way. A claim about the unseen is met not with a counterargument but with a question about attendance.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God sets a standard here that is about procedure before it is about content. Where a rule came from is asked before whether the rule is right. That is uncomfortable in every generation, because much of what any community treats as required arrived without an occasion anyone can name. The clause about misleading others is what makes the judgement so severe. A made-up rule does not stay with the person who made it.

crossReferences.why: Asks the same question of another claim, whether they witnessed the creation of what they describe.
States the same judgement earlier in this surah, on inventing against God or denying His signs.
Names the practice directly, tongues calling things allowed or withheld and inventing about God.

studies.applyIt: Take one religious practice you keep and ask whether you could say where it comes from, in a sentence, to someone who asked sincerely. If you cannot, that is a research task and not a reason to stop. The question in this verse is about sources. Knowing yours tends to make a practice steadier rather than shakier.
studies.explainEasier: Ask the same about camels and cattle. Were you standing there when God told you to do this. Nobody does worse than a person who makes up lies about God to lead people astray.

studies.title: Nothing That I Find
studies.meaning: The answer to a long argument is a report, not a ruling. In what was revealed to him he does not find anything held back from someone eating, apart from a short and specific list. Early scholars pay attention to that wording. It describes searching what was given and saying what is there, so nothing is being decided on the spot. And the verse does not close with a warning. Someone driven to it by need, without going looking for it or overstepping, is met with two names of mercy.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, and this is the surah's direct answer to the customs it has spent so long describing. The list is short, and other passages in the Quran give it in nearly the same terms. The scholars discuss how they relate at length. What everyone agrees on is the contrast being drawn. An elaborate inherited system sits on one side, and a brief answer on the other.

keyTerms.note: The verb for finding something on searching. Reporting a search rather than issuing a decision keeps the speaker in the position of a reader of what was given, which the whole surah has insisted on.
From a root for raising the voice, which also gives the word for a new crescent moon greeted with shouts. It names the act of announcing a name aloud, which is what makes the dedication meaningful.
Two names that close many Quranic passages where a limit has just been stated. The first covers what is concealed and pardoned, the second a mercy that is given rather than earned.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Necessity was not a thought experiment here. Famine years, a caravan that ran short, a family cut off by drought: these put people in front of decisions they would never otherwise face. The sources describe communities in real starvation. So the clause about compulsion was not added for an unusual case. It answered a situation many in the audience had already seen, or would.
studies.didYouKnow: This same short list turns up in four places across the Quran, in Meccan and Medinan surahs alike, and every one of them carries the same clause about the person compelled by need. That kind of consistency is unusual. Early scholars treat the repeated exception as part of the list rather than as an afterthought.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The shortness is the argument. After many verses describing customs added by vow and inheritance, the answer is brief enough to hold in your head. That says something about the difference between what was given and what gathered around it. Then the two names at the end govern everything before them. A limit that ends in forgiveness and mercy is a different kind of thing from one that ends in a threat, and the verse puts them in that order.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same short list with the same exception, in another Meccan setting.
Repeats the list and the clause about being compelled, adding that God is forgiving and merciful.
Sets out the fullest version in a Medinan surah, ending again with the exception for need.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone you know who is in a hard spot and has done something you would not do. Before you judge it, ask what their options actually were. This verse attaches an exception for need to the limit it states. Extend the same courtesy to a person you know. It costs a moment of imagination and very little else.
studies.explainEasier: In what was sent down to me I find only a short list of food to keep away from. It is dead meat, flowing blood, pork, and meat named for someone other than God. If you are forced by need, your Lord forgives.

studies.title: That Was Their Recompense
studies.meaning: A different and much longer set of limits is described here, given to an earlier community. The verse is careful about which parts were included and which were not, and early scholars notice that care. The exceptions are named as exactly as the restrictions. The reason is stated plainly. This came as a repayment for a particular overstepping, so the limits were a consequence rather than a permanent feature of things. God then says that the account itself is true.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, and the comparison is drawn for the people standing in front of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). The surah has just described customs invented with no authority behind them. Here it describes limits that had a source and a stated reason. Other passages in the Quran give the same restrictions in similar terms. The early commentaries read the accounts together.

keyTerms.note: The word for a claw or an undivided hoof, and the commentators differ over how widely it extends. The range of their readings is preserved rather than settled, which is characteristic of the vocabulary here.
The plural of a word for animal fat, a valuable food in a lean economy. Naming the exceptions in detail keeps the restriction bounded rather than sweeping, which is the ayah's evident concern.
From a root for seeking and then for exceeding a limit. It names a specific transgression rather than a character, which is why the ayah gives a reason instead of a verdict on a people.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Communities following earlier scriptures lived across the region and in Arabian towns. They traded and farmed next to their neighbours, and their food practices were visible and well known. Meccans travelling north met them on the road often. So the audience for this verse already knew the limits being described here. That is why they could be named with no explanation attached.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran describes these limits in two other places, and one of them adds a detail worth pausing on. All food had been allowed before, apart from what one forefather had withheld from himself. Read together, the three passages show the limits arising inside history rather than standing there from the start.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The verse draws a line that everything around it depends on. Limits can come from God, and then they have a source, a scope and a reason. Or they can gather over time with none of the three. Naming a cause for these limits keeps them understandable instead of arbitrary. The statement of truthfulness at the end attaches to the account, which the surah offers as something you can check rather than something to take on trust.

crossReferences.why: Notes that food had been permitted before, apart from what one forefather withheld from himself.
Describes the same limits and gives the same reason, naming the conduct behind them.
Refers back to this passage and adds that the wrong done was to themselves rather than to God.

studies.applyIt: Think of a restriction you live under that arrived as a consequence of something: a rule at work after an incident, a limit in a relationship after a breach.
