Ask whether the reason still holds. Rules that come with reasons can be revisited. This verse is careful to give one, and that is what makes revisiting possible.
studies.explainEasier: For the Jewish people God banned every animal with claws, and much of the fat of cattle and sheep. That was a payback for a wrong they had done. God tells the truth.

studies.title: Mercy Wide, Yet Not Averted
studies.meaning: Being called a liar is a hard thing to live with, and the instruction given here is not a defence. Tell them their Lord holds a mercy that is wide, and then add the rest without softening either part. Early scholars note the order. Mercy is named first and at greater length, and the word used for its width is the one used elsewhere for knowledge that takes everything in. The words at the end state a limit that is about direction rather than severity. What is coming is not turned back from those who have earned it.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, where the charge of lying was not occasional but constant. The surah has already recorded it in several forms. Putting a statement about mercy into the mouth of a man just called a liar is a striking choice. The early sources treat it as typical of the Meccan years. Again and again, the answer to hostility was a description of God rather than a rebuttal.

keyTerms.note: From the verb for containing something with room to spare, used earlier in this surah of God's knowledge. Applied to mercy it says the same thing: nothing falls outside for lack of capacity.
A passive verb for something sent back the way it came. The denial is about deflection rather than about force, so what is described is a consequence that cannot be redirected once it is moving.
From a root for cutting or severing, connected to harvesting. The word names people by their acts rather than by their beliefs, which keeps the category defined by conduct.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A protector in Arabia could shelter a man from consequences. The whole system of clan patronage worked by turning claims aside, and a powerful patron could make a debt or a blood claim simply stop. Everyone listening knew that the question was rarely whether you were guilty. It was whether someone would stand between you and the claim. The verse speaks straight into that expectation.
studies.didYouKnow: An assurance of mercy paired with a statement of consequence turns up again and again in the Quran. Often the pair sits inside one verse, and the mercy is almost always named first. The early commentaries treat that order as deliberate. Hope is set down before any limit is described.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Both halves land on the same audience in the same breath. That cuts against the instinct to sort people into those who need encouraging and those who need warning, since the verse assumes one listener can hold both. The word used for the width of mercy matters too. It does not say mercy is large enough for most cases. It says capacity was never the constraint, which moves the question somewhere else entirely.

crossReferences.why: States the same width directly, that His mercy covers everything there is.
Puts the assurance in its most open form, spoken to those who went furthest against themselves.
Places forgiveness, acceptance of repentance and severity together in one run of names.

studies.applyIt: Notice which half of this you usually reach for. Some of us comfort people and some of us warn them, and most of us lean one way while calling it balance. Once this week, say the half you would normally leave out, inside the same conversation. This verse gives both to the same listener in one sentence.
studies.explainEasier: If they call you a liar, tell them this. Your Lord has mercy wide enough for everyone. But what is coming for guilty people cannot be turned away.

studies.title: Had God Willed, We Would Not
studies.meaning: The objection is quoted before it is even made, and it is the best one they have. If God had willed otherwise, none of this would have happened, so what we do must be what He wanted. Early scholars note that the verse does not deny the premise. It observes that earlier peoples argued in exactly the same way, and that the argument did not protect them when the consequence came. Then it asks for the one thing the objection lacks: knowledge that can be brought out and shown. What is left is guesswork.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, and this argument was in live use in the streets. The surah itself has said more than once that God could have gathered everyone onto guidance. So the objectors were quoting a principle the message had taught them. The early scholars read the answer as addressing the use being made of a true statement, not the statement itself.

keyTerms.note: The verb of tasting used through this surah for consequence experienced directly. Its appearance here marks the end of the earlier peoples' argument, which was not refuted but simply overtaken by events.

keyTerms.gloss: so you may bring it out
keyTerms.note: A verb for producing something from where it is kept, as goods are brought out for inspection. The demand is for evidence to be shown rather than described, which is what an appeal to knowledge means here.
The technical term for assessing a standing crop by eye, used earlier in this surah of the majority. Its return here labels a theological argument with a word from agricultural approximation.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Fate was a serious idea in Arabia before Islam. The poetry hands deaths, losses and fortunes over to time or to fate, and the habit ran deep enough to shape how people talked about their own choices. So the objection recorded here was not invented for the occasion. It drew on a long practice of explaining what had happened by saying it was always going to happen.
studies.didYouKnow: This objection is quoted in at least three places in the Quran, in almost the same words each time, and it is never answered by denying that God's will governs events. The reply always turns on what the speakers can actually produce. The same argument gets the same handling across separate surahs.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The verse separates a truth from the use people make of it. That God's will governs what happens is said throughout the Quran, including a few verses further on. What the objectors do is turn it into a defence. The answer points out that they have no access to the premise they are leaning on. Nobody gets to consult God's will in advance, so it cannot serve as a reason for a course already chosen.

crossReferences.why: Records the same objection almost word for word, and answers by saying what messengers were for.
Preserves another version of it, adding that they have no knowledge of what they assert.
Follows immediately and grants the premise itself, that He could have guided everyone.

studies.applyIt: Catch yourself explaining a choice by saying it was meant to be, or that you had no option. Sometimes that is true, and saying so costs nothing. Once today, when you hear yourself say it, ask what you would have done differently had you believed the choice was yours. The answer usually arrives straight away.
studies.explainEasier: They say that if God had wanted, they would not have worshipped anything else, and they would not have banned any food. People before them said the same and then felt what came. Ask them to show what they actually know.

studies.title: The Conclusive Argument
studies.meaning: Two short lines, and the second one grants exactly what the objectors had just claimed. The conclusive argument belongs to God, and had He willed, He would have guided every one of you. Early scholars point to the word used for that argument. It names the case that reaches its destination and ends a dispute. What is denied is not the premise but who owns it. The objectors were using God's will as their argument. The answer is that the argument which arrives is His.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, set down immediately after the objection it answers. The surah has been building a case for many verses, and this is close to its last word on who can settle the matter. No occasion is reported for it. The pairing of the two verses, objection and then answer, is one of the clearest examples of this surah quoting an argument in full before replying to it.

keyTerms.note: The decisive case in a dispute, the same word used earlier in this surah of the reasoning given to Abraham. Both times it is described as belonging to God rather than to the person making it.
From the verb for arriving at a destination, used earlier in this surah of the recitation reaching whomever it reaches. An argument described this way is one that gets all the way there.
An emphatic word for totality placed at the end for weight. It closes off any reading in which some would have been guided and others left, which is the softening a listener might have looked for.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A dispute in Arabia ended when one side produced a case the other could not answer. Everyone present knew that moment when it came. The word for such an argument was in ordinary use in the markets and the councils. So saying that the conclusive one belongs to God described the end of a hearing, not a stage in it. An audience used to settling things in the open heard exactly that.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a conclusive argument shows up only a handful of times in the Quran, and one of them explains why messengers were sent at all. It was so that people would have no argument against God afterwards. The same term marks both what God holds and what human beings are left without.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The verse states the uncomfortable premise instead of dodging it, which is what makes the answer before it honest. God could have guided everyone and did not. What is refused is the step from that fact to a defence. Nobody can lean on a decision they were not part of. So the verse concedes everything about God's will and nothing at all about what people answer for.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word, saying messengers were sent so that no argument would remain against God.
States the same conditional about people being made one community, and what followed instead.
Holds both sides in two lines: whoever wills may take a way, and the willing sits inside God's will.

studies.applyIt: Notice the difference between accepting that something was in God's hands after it happens, and using that to decide what to do beforehand. The first is trust and the second is not. Pick one decision you are facing and make it on the reasons available to you, then hand the outcome over afterwards. That order is the one this verse keeps.
studies.explainEasier: The final proof belongs to God. If He had wanted to, He could have guided every single one of you. That is what it says, and it says nothing more.

studies.title: Bring Your Witnesses Forward
studies.meaning: The challenge becomes a summons. Bring your witnesses, the ones who will swear that God withheld this. Then comes an instruction that expects them to turn up: if they testify, do not testify with them. Early scholars note the assumption built into that sentence. Witnesses could well be produced, and their number would prove nothing. The verse then says three things about the people whose leanings are not to be followed, and each one is a description rather than an insult.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, and the summons borrows the language of Arabian dispute settlement. A claim there was backed by producing men who would swear to it, and numbers and standing counted for more than what those men had actually seen. The surah has been asking for a source for these customs across many verses. This is the last and most formal version of the request.

keyTerms.note: An imperative of summoning, unchanged for number or gender in the dialect the Quran preserves. Its abruptness gives the challenge the tone of a courtroom rather than of a discussion.
A prohibition against joining a testimony, not against hearing it. It separates the act of witnessing from the act of being present, which is the distinction on which the whole instruction rests.
The same verb that closes the very first ayah of this surah, where those who refuse set up equals to their Lord. Its return here brings the surah's argument back to where it began.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Producing witnesses was how a case was won. A man with more supporters, and supporters of higher standing, carried the day. What they swore to often mattered less than who they were, so testimony was an act of taking sides as much as of reporting. That is exactly why the instruction here separates being in the room from adding your own voice to what is said.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb that closes this verse is the same one that closes the opening verse of the surah, where those who refuse set up equals to their Lord. More than a hundred and forty verses apart, the two uses frame the whole argument. The surah's closing challenge comes back to the word it began with.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Truthfulness is treated as something separate from agreement, and the instruction makes that separation workable. Others may testify. You are not asked to contradict them, only not to join in. That is a form of integrity someone outnumbered can actually keep, and being outnumbered is what the audience for this verse was. The passage also ties following leanings to not expecting a hereafter. What a person can afford to say depends on what they expect.

crossReferences.why: Describes standing firm as witnesses for God even against oneself or one's own relatives.
Asks who does greater wrong than the one who hides a testimony he holds from God.
Asks the same question a few verses earlier, whether they were present when this was enjoined.

studies.applyIt: Think of the last time a group settled on something you did not believe, and you nodded along. This verse does not ask you to argue. It asks you not to add your own voice to it, which is a smaller and much more reachable thing. Practise the silence once, and notice how little it actually costs.
studies.explainEasier: Ask them to bring people who will swear that God banned this. If they do swear, do not swear along with them. Do not follow people who turn away from God's signs.

studies.title: Come, I Will Recite It
studies.meaning: This is the reply to a long quarrel about what people had banned on their own say-so. Come, and I will read you what your Lord actually forbade. The words are recited rather than argued out. Most of the items are things to keep away from, with one positive charge in the middle about honouring parents. Killing children out of poverty is answered inside the same sentence with a promise of provision. Early scholars note that indecency is named in both its open and its hidden forms.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, at the end of a surah that has spent its length arguing with people about what they had declared off limits on their own authority. The verses just before it challenge those home-made bans. This passage answers by reading out what was actually laid down. Early scholars treat the order as deliberate. A false list is set aside, and a true one is read in its place.

keyTerms.note: An imperative meaning to come towards a higher place, used to call someone over. It opens the passage as an invitation rather than a summons, and it is addressed to opponents in the middle of a dispute.
Not general hardship but the condition of having nothing left at all. The word names the actual pressure behind the practice being addressed, which the verse answers by naming who provides.
The plural of a word for what is excessive and shameful. The verse divides it into what appears and what is hidden, so the category is defined by the act rather than by whether anyone saw it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Burying an infant in a famine year is attested in the poetry and the reports of Arabia before Islam. It was driven by the sums of a bad season. In a household with nothing in reserve there were mouths that could not be fed. The Quran comes back to this practice more than once, and every time it ties a word about provision to the ban. That answers the sum and not only the act.
studies.didYouKnow: This passage and the two verses after it have been read since early times as a parallel to the commandments given to Moses, and the classical scholars note the resemblance outright. The list here starts where those start, with setting up nothing beside God and honouring parents. It ends with a call to understand rather than with a threat.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The list arrives as recitation, which puts its authority outside the man speaking it. That is the whole weight of the surah's argument. There is a difference between what God laid down and what a community settled on among itself. Setting kindness to parents inside a run of prohibitions has been read a particular way. Some duties cannot be met by holding back alone. The purpose named at the end is understanding.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the ban on killing children from fear of poverty, turning the order of provision around.
Continues the same recitation through weights, speech, and the straight path.
Lists what has actually been forbidden, open indecency and hidden alike.

studies.applyIt: This verse divides wrongdoing into what shows and what does not. Pick the quietest item on your own list, the thing nobody would ever hear about, and do one concrete thing this week that makes carrying on with it harder. Not a resolution, an arrangement. The hidden half is the half that lives on being unmentioned.
studies.explainEasier: God tells the Prophet to read out what God has really forbidden. The list says not to set anything beside God, to be good to your parents, and not to kill your children out of poverty. God feeds you all.

studies.title: Even If It Concerns A Relative
studies.meaning: Four things sit together here, and the grouping is deliberate. Property held for a child who cannot yet defend it. Weights and measures at the market stall. What you say about someone, and the covenant with God. Early scholars note the clause dropped into the middle, that no soul is charged beyond what it can carry, which eases the standard for measuring without lowering it. The hardest of the four is fairness in speech, because it is asked even when a close relative is involved.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, part of a short run of verses that reads like a summary of what was really enjoined, set against the customs the surah has just taken apart. Orphans were numerous in a society where men died young in raids and on journeys. Their property passed into the keeping of relatives, with nobody outside looking on. Measures at the seasonal fairs went unpoliced in much the same way.

keyTerms.note: From the root for firmness and strength, naming the age at which a person can manage their own affairs. Commentators differ over the exact point, and the tradition records a range of readings.
A word for a share correctly apportioned, distinct from the general term for justice. Its root sense is dividing something into due portions, which suits an instruction about weights and measures.
From the root for balance and equality, the same one used at the surah's opening for setting up equals to God. Applied to speech it asks for an account that does not lean.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Weights and measures were personal property. A merchant carried his own stones and his own measuring vessel. A small gap between the set he used for buying and the set he used for selling was invisible and profitable. Orphans' estates were held on the same trust, with no register kept anywhere. Both arrangements ran entirely on the character of the person holding them.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause about no soul being burdened beyond what it can bear turns up three times in the Quran, and here it sits in the middle of an instruction about measuring. That placement is unusual. The classical scholars read it as granting that perfect exactness in a weighing is not reachable, while honest intent is.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Every item names a situation where nobody would find out. A child cannot audit an estate. A customer cannot check a stone. An account given about a relative is checked against nothing. Putting the covenant with God at the end of that list is the argument of the whole verse. What holds in unwatched places is a relationship rather than a rule, and that is why the four belong in one sentence.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same pair almost word for word, orphan property and full measure with a straight balance.
Describes the exact fraud named here, taking full measure from others and giving less in return.
Extends fairness in testimony to cases against oneself, parents and near relatives alike.

studies.applyIt: Think of the last time you described a disagreement involving someone close to you. Tell it again, to yourself, giving the other side's version the same room. That is the third item on this list, and it is the one most of us fail without noticing, because nobody is ever there to check the account.
studies.explainEasier: Do not touch what belongs to an orphan, except to help, until he grows up. Give full weight and full measure when you sell. Be fair when you speak, even about your own family, and keep your promise to God.

studies.title: One Path And Many Ways
studies.meaning: One road is named and the others are not. The path is single and called straight, while the alternatives are plural and left nameless. Following them, the verse says, scatters you away from His way. Early scholars note that the verb describes a group being pulled apart rather than one person losing their bearings. Nothing at all is said about where the other ways lead. What is named is only what taking them does, which is breaking people up. The purpose given at the end is care.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, closing the short run of what was actually enjoined. The surah has spent its last stretch describing customs that had drifted off in different directions, so a warning about many ways answers something concrete rather than abstract. The classical scholars record a report about the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). He drew a single line, with shorter lines branching off it, to show what this verse meant.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word for a track or route, set against the singular term used for the path. Arabic marks the contrast by number alone, which the translation has to do with an adjective.
An intensive verb for a group breaking into separate pieces. The object is the people rather than the road, so what the other routes do first is divide those walking, not mislead them.
The same verb that closes the two ayat before this one, marking the end of each instruction. Its repetition binds the short sequence together as a single charge rather than three separate ones.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A caravan held together by staying on one route. Where the tracks branched, a party that split at a fork could lose contact for days, or for good, and there was no way to signal across that distance. Guides argued about routes, and the arguments mattered. Everyone travelling in that country understood that the danger at a fork was separation long before it was the wrong destination.
studies.didYouKnow: The classical collections keep a report of the Prophet drawing a straight line in the sand and then short lines branching off it. He said the first was the way, and pointed at the others as paths with something calling from each of them. The image is remembered mainly because it explains this verse.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Unity is shown as the result of direction rather than as a separate duty, which is a striking thing to claim. People are not told to hold together and also to follow the path. Following the path is what holds them together. Leaving it is described first by what it does to the group. The purpose named at the end is care rather than correctness, which keeps the instruction from turning into a matter of position alone.

crossReferences.why: Names the same single way given across the prophets, and warns against becoming divided in it.
Uses the same shape: a way ordained to be followed, against the leanings of those without knowledge.
Turns the same straight path into the request recited in every unit of the daily prayer.

studies.applyIt: Notice a disagreement in your community that is about method rather than about anything at its heart. Ask what it would take for both sides to keep walking together while they still disagree. The first warning in this verse is about scattering. The cost of a branch is usually paid in company, and only later in direction.
studies.explainEasier: This is My path, and it is straight, so follow it. Do not follow the other roads, because they will pull you away from His path. God tells you this so you will stay careful.

studies.title: Complete For The One Who Did Well
studies.meaning: Four things are said about the Book given to Moses, and the first one is the least expected. It was a completion for the person who did well. Early scholars read that in more than one way. It may mean completing what such a person already held, or a favour brought to its full state, and the tradition keeps both. The other three are detail, guidance and mercy. The purpose named at the end is belief in meeting their Lord, which is the very thing this surah has been arguing for all along.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, and Moses is brought in here to serve the argument. The audience accepted that an earlier Book existed and was known across the region. The verses that follow use that acceptance to take away an excuse. The classical sources attach no occasion to this verse. Scholars have read the Arabic word that opens it as marking order in the telling rather than order in time.

keyTerms.note: A verbal noun for bringing something to its full state. Read either as completing a favour or as completing what was already held, and the classical commentaries record both without deciding.
From the root for beauty and excellence, so the verb means doing something well rather than merely doing it. The same root gave this surah its word for the prophets in the earlier list.

keyTerms.gloss: and a setting out in detail
keyTerms.note: The noun from the verb used repeatedly in this surah for separating something into its parts. Applied to a scripture it describes a text laid out so that its pieces can be distinguished.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Communities holding the earlier scripture lived along the trade roads north and in the towns of Arabia, and Meccan merchants dealt with them all the time. That a Book had been given to Moses was common knowledge in the region rather than a claim needing support. Nobody argued about it. That is exactly why the case built on it in the verses that follow works.
studies.didYouKnow: This verse and the one after it use nearly the same words for two different scriptures. Each is described as sent down, and each is described as carrying guidance and mercy. Setting the two descriptions side by side is how the surah shows they belong together, without ever arguing the point.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Revelation is shown here finishing something rather than replacing it, and what it finishes belongs to a person who was already doing well. That order matters. The Book meets goodness that is there and completes it rather than making it from nothing. The aim stated at the end is belief in meeting their Lord. That ties a whole scripture to the one thing this surah has defended since its opening.

crossReferences.why: Names the same giving, the Scripture and the criterion, so that they might be guided.
Refers to the same Book and makes it a reason not to doubt the meeting being described.
Describes it as guidance and a reminder inherited by those who came after him.

studies.applyIt: Think of a good habit you already keep that could be finished rather than swapped out. Giving that has no rhythm to it, or reading with no aim in mind. This verse describes a gift completed for someone already doing well. Add the missing piece to one such habit this week instead of starting a new one.
studies.explainEasier: Then We gave Moses the Book. It was a full gift for the one who did good, and it explained everything. It was a light and a mercy, so that people would believe they will meet their Lord.

studies.title: Lest You Should Say
studies.meaning: The reason given for this Book is stated backwards, and that is unusual. It came so that one particular sentence could no longer be said. The sentence runs like this. Scripture was given to two communities before us, and we knew nothing of what they studied. Early scholars identify the two as the communities holding the earlier scriptures. What is being taken away is not disbelief but distance. It is the fair complaint of people who had heard that revelation existed somewhere else and had never received any in their own language.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, and the complaint was a real one. Arabs knew that scriptural communities existed nearby, and knew those scriptures were studied in languages they could not read. Some in the region had already begun looking for something of their own before the message came. The passage answers a genuine grievance rather than an imagined one, which is why it is met by removal rather than by rebuke.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to kneel and settle, giving the idea of good that comes to rest in a place. The same description was applied to this Book earlier in the surah, in a passage about warning a city.
A dual form for two distinct parties, from a root meaning to go around something. The dual is precise: the complaint named two known communities rather than scripture-holders in general.
From the root for reading a text repeatedly until it is learned, the same verb used earlier in this surah in the accusation that he had studied. The word names sustained schooling in a text.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Scripture was studied out loud in languages Arabs did not know. A Meccan trader in a northern town would see a group gathered around a reader working through a text he could not follow. He would know that something weighty was being handled there, and that it was closed to him. That scene, repeated over the years, is the very complaint these verses quote.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for study comes from the same root as the verb in an accusation a few pages earlier, where people said the Prophet had been taught by someone. So the same term shows up twice in this surah. Once it is a charge thrown at him. Once it sits inside the excuse his people would have made without him.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Revelation is described as closing an excuse, which puts the whole subject inside fairness rather than favour. Nobody is to answer for what was only ever there in a language and a people not their own. That is a claim about how God deals with everyone. And it carries something further with it. Wherever a real excuse of not knowing exists, it is treated as real.

crossReferences.why: Describes this same Book in nearly identical words earlier in the surah, with a different purpose attached.
Names the earlier scriptures given before, which the two communities in this complaint held.
Voices the same excuse from the other end, asking why no messenger was sent before the consequence.

studies.applyIt: Notice an excuse you use that happens to be true: not enough time, never taught, nobody showed you. Some of them are fair. Pick one and ask what would have to change for it to stop being available to you. These verses take a real excuse seriously and then remove it, which is a different thing from brushing it aside.
studies.explainEasier: This Book is a blessed one that We sent down, so follow it. Then you cannot say that a Book was given to two groups before you. You cannot say you never knew what they were reading.

studies.title: We Would Have Been Better Guided
studies.meaning: The second excuse is confidence rather than ignorance. Had a Book come to us, we would have made better use of it than they did. Early scholars note the tone of that, which assumes the earlier communities failed through some flaw the speakers do not have. The answer comes without any argument. Clarification has now come, and guidance, and mercy, so the claim can be tested instead of merely stated. The rest of the verse names what turning away from it amounts to.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, and this sentiment is recorded elsewhere in the Quran as an oath sworn before the message arrived. They swore that if a warner reached them they would be better guided than any nation. The surah quotes the boast after the message has come, and that changes what it is. It is no longer a claim about a possibility. It describes what did not happen.

keyTerms.note: A comparative from the root for finding a way. Comparing one's own hypothetical performance to another community's actual record is the exact form the ayah is quoting, and the comparative carries it.

Something that makes a matter plain, the same word used earlier in this surah when the speaker says he stands on clear evidence from his Lord. Its return here places the same thing in the listeners' hands.

A less common verb for veering away, used earlier in this surah of people shying from the signs. It is repeated three times in this one ayah, which is unusual and makes turning away the sentence's subject.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabs took great pride in their memory and their language. Holding poetry and family lines in the head was treated as proof of a better mind. A community that could carry thousands of lines of verse without writing had reason to think it would handle a text well. So the boast quoted here was not empty vanity. It rested on a real and provable skill.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for turning aside occurs three times in this one verse, in three different forms, and it appears nowhere in the Quran outside this surah. That concentration is deliberate. The words at the end say the repayment matches the turning away, using the same term for both sides of it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A claim about imagined performance is answered by handing over the actual test. Anyone can be confident about what they would do in a situation they are not in. The verse quietly points out that the situation has now arrived. The one verb repeated at the end makes a further point about matching. What comes back to a person matches what they did, and the same word carries both.

crossReferences.why: Records the same boast as a solemn oath, sworn before any warner had reached them.
States the same test earlier in this surah, that insights have come and the seeing is each person's own.
Names the excuse this removes, that they would have asked why no messenger was sent to them.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you are sure you would handle better than the person currently handling it. Now recall a time you were given exactly that chance and did about as well as anybody else. Hold the two together for a minute. This verse answers an imagined case by pointing at the real one.
studies.explainEasier: Or you might say that if a Book had come to you, you would have followed it better than they did. But clear proof has now come to you. It came from your Lord, with guidance and mercy.

studies.title: Faith That Comes Too Late
studies.meaning: Three arrivals are named as things they might be waiting for, and then one of them is followed through. On the day some of your Lord's signs come, faith will not help a soul that had not believed already, or earned some good through its believing. Early scholars discuss which sign is meant and record several readings. What the verse marks out is a closing point. After it, belief is no longer an answer to anything. It is a reaction to what has become impossible to miss.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, near the end of the surah, and the demand for one decisive sign has run all the way through it. The audience had asked for angels, and for God Himself to appear. This verse takes the request seriously enough to describe what would follow if it were granted. The classical scholars connect it to a wider Quranic account of belief offered at the last moment.

keyTerms.note: The verb for looking and for waiting, used earlier in this surah for the respite granted to people. Waiting and being given time are the same word, which gives the question its edge.

The commercial verb used at the opening of this surah for what God knows of a person. Its appearance here adds a second condition, so belief alone without anything earned through it is not the picture described.
An imperative from the same root as the verb for waiting at the ayah's start. The instruction returns their own posture to them, and the speaker joins it rather than standing outside it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Debt in Arabia ran to a named day. A creditor could extend it, but the moment the term ran out the whole arrangement changed. What had been a bargain became a claim. Everyone understood that a payment offered the day before and the day after were two different acts, and that goodwill did not survive the line. The words for waiting and for respite come out of that world.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran describes belief arriving too late more than once, and one case is a tyrant declaring his faith as the water closes over him. Each account is built the same way. The words are correct and the timing is not, and the passage says plainly that the words no longer do anything.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A limit is set on repentance here, and it is about knowledge rather than harshness. Faith held while the outcome is still uncertain is one act. Agreement given once the outcome is on display is another, and only the first is what was asked for. The second condition is just as striking. Belief is expected to have produced something, so the verse measures a life rather than a moment of conviction.

crossReferences.why: States the same limit for repentance offered at the moment death arrives, when nothing is uncertain.
Narrates the clearest instance, a declaration of faith made as the sea closes over the speaker.
Describes faith declared on seeing the punishment, and says it did not benefit them then.

studies.applyIt: Think of a good decision you keep putting off while you wait for things to make it obvious. It might be a resignation, a reconciliation, or a change in how you live. The worth of choosing now lies in the fact that it is not yet obvious. This verse marks the line between choosing and giving in. The window for the first one closes quietly.
studies.explainEasier: Are they just waiting for angels to come, or for their Lord, or for some sign of His. On the day a sign like that comes, believing then will not help. It only helps those who believed before.

studies.title: You Have No Part In That
studies.meaning: Two things are described together, and the second grows out of the first. They broke their religion into pieces, and then they became parties. Early scholars note that the breaking is named before the factions, so the groups are the result and not the cause. The instruction is a full separation from the activity, not from the people. The reason given is about who holds the case. Their matter rests with God, who will tell them what they were doing. That settles who does the sorting.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, near the surah's end, and the classical scholars differ over who is being described. Some read it of earlier communities whose unity had come apart. Others read it as a general statement covering anyone who does this. The tradition keeps the range open. The surah has already warned against following many ways instead of one, and this verse names what that leads to.

keyTerms.note: An intensive verb for separating something into fragments. The object is their religion, so what is described is damage to a single thing rather than a disagreement between people about it.

The same word used earlier in this surah, where being split into factions is listed among afflictions God is able to send. Its return here makes the condition a consequence rather than only a punishment.
A word covering a matter, a command and a decision at once. Assigning it to God removes the case from human hands entirely, which is the ground of the instruction that precedes it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian society was built out of groups that fought for standing, and a man's name came from whichever one claimed him. Splits inside a tribe were common. They left long feuds over who came first and who inherited what. Everyone knew what it looked like when one body became several. They knew how fast the line between them became the main fact about anybody.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for factions in this verse appears earlier in the same surah, sitting in a list of what God is able to send upon a people. It stands there alongside afflictions from above and below. So one term names a punishment in one passage and a self-inflicted condition in the other, and the vocabulary does not change.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The verse separates the activity from the people doing it, and that separation is what makes the instruction liveable. Judgement is placed with God, plainly, so what is asked of you is only that you not join in. That is narrower than it first sounds. It leaves your relationships intact and lifts the duty to judge between groups off your shoulders. What you keep clear of is the breaking apart itself.

crossReferences.why: Warns against becoming like those who divided and differed after clear proofs had reached them.
Describes the same outcome, an affair cut into pieces with each party pleased by its own portion.
Gives the instruction this condition follows from, one path rather than many scattering ways.

studies.applyIt: Notice a dispute inside your own community that you were drawn into by loyalty rather than conviction. Step out of the argument for a month without stepping away from anyone in it. This verse puts the judging somewhere else. It asks only that you not join the breaking, and that is something you can do quietly.
studies.explainEasier: Some people broke their religion into pieces and split into groups. You have nothing to do with that. Their case is with God, and He will tell them later what they were doing.

studies.title: Ten For One
studies.meaning: The rate of exchange is stated plainly, and it is not an even one. A good deed brought in is answered tenfold. A bad one is answered with its like and no more. Early scholars look closely at both halves. The good is multiplied, and elsewhere in the Quran the ceiling is left open. The bad is held down by a word meaning equal measure. The last words explain why that imbalance is not unfair. Nobody receives less than they earned.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, near the end of a surah taken up mostly with argument and warning. Its last verses turn from dispute to a statement of terms, and this is one of them. Early scholars record no occasion for it, and they read the placement as deliberate. After a long quarrel about what people had invented, the surah closes by setting out how the account is actually kept.

keyTerms.note: The verb for arriving carrying something, rather than for doing it. It pictures the deed as an item brought to a counter, which is why the response is described as a rate rather than as a verdict.

The multiplier is stated as ten likenesses of the thing itself, not ten of something else. What is returned keeps the shape of what was given, magnified rather than exchanged for a different currency.

The passive of the verb for putting something out of its place. Its use here defines fairness as receiving no less than what is due, which leaves the extra given to a good deed outside the calculation.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan trade ran on rates of exchange, and everybody there understood a multiplier. A merchant paid for a caravan expecting several times his money to come back. Profit was reckoned in shares agreed before anyone set out. Putting the moral account in that language used terms the audience handled every day. The tenfold figure was heard as a rate of return, not as a picture.
studies.didYouKnow: Elsewhere the Quran raises the multiplier far beyond ten. One passage compares a good deed to a grain that produces seven ears with a hundred grains in each, and adds that God multiplies further for whom He wills. So the ten here is the floor of what is promised, not the limit. Early scholars read the two passages together.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The imbalance is the teaching. If mercy is written into the accounting itself, then hope is not a mood you have to work up. It is a fact about the ledger. Capping the penalty at equal measure keeps justice whole, so the generosity costs nothing in fairness. Between them the two halves describe a system tilted one way on purpose, and the tilt is stated as policy rather than as a favour.

crossReferences.why: Raises the same multiplying far higher with the image of a grain and seven ears.
States that God does not wrong by an atom's weight and doubles a good deed.
Repeats the same lopsidedness in a Meccan surah, with better than the deed for the good.

studies.applyIt: Do one small good thing today that you would normally skip because it looks too minor to count. A message of thanks, or a plate washed that is not yours. The whole argument of this verse is about scale, and it says the scale is not yours to judge. Your part is the bringing.
studies.explainEasier: If you do one good thing, God gives you ten times as much back. If you do one bad thing, it counts as one, and no more. Nobody is treated unfairly.

studies.title: The Creed Of Abraham
studies.meaning: The declaration is personal and it builds. My Lord has guided me. Then four descriptions stack up: a straight path, an upright religion, the creed of Abraham, a man inclining toward truth. Early scholars note the word for that inclination. It names a turning away from everything else and a turning toward one thing in the same motion. The sharpest part comes last. Abraham is the ancestor this audience claimed, and the verse says plainly that he was not among those who set up partners.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, and the appeal to Abraham was an appeal to the audience's own family tree. The families of Mecca traced their descent from him and kept custody of a sanctuary they linked with him. Their religious practice was defended as inherited from that source. Naming his creed and then denying that it ever included setting up partners cut straight across the claim.

keyTerms.note: From the root for standing, so a religion described this way is one that stands straight and holds others up. The same root gives the verb used elsewhere for establishing the prayer.
A word for the path a community follows, distinct from the general term for religion. It carries a founder's name naturally, which is why the Quran uses it whenever Abraham is being invoked.

From a root meaning to turn away from something and toward another. Pre-Islamic Arabia knew individuals described by this word who had abandoned the local practices without joining any other community.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The sources record a small number of men in Mecca and the country around it who had rejected the local rites before the message came. They went looking for the religion of Abraham, and some travelled as far as Syria in the search. They were known, and thought odd rather than dangerous. The word this verse uses for inclining was the term people applied to them.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing Abraham here turns up about a dozen times in the Quran, and in almost every case a denial follows at once. He associated nothing with God. The pairing is so steady that the classical scholars treat the second half as part of what the term means.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A claim of inheritance is answered with a claim about content. Descent from Abraham is not in dispute. What is in dispute is whether the practice being defended is actually his. That move splits a tradition from the man it is credited to, and it can be made about any handed-down religion. The list also puts guidance first, as something received, before any of the words that follow it.

crossReferences.why: Answers a competing claim with the same phrase, the creed of Abraham, inclining toward truth.
Issues the same instruction to follow that creed, closing with the identical denial about partners.
Describes him as a community in himself, thankful and chosen, and guided to a straight path.

studies.applyIt: Take one practice you keep because it belongs to your tradition, and check it against the person or the period the tradition names. Not to drop it if it does not match. Just to know which parts you can trace and which arrived later. This verse makes exactly that distinction about a lineage everyone in the room shared.
studies.explainEasier: My Lord has shown me a straight path. It is a true and upright religion, the way of Abraham, who turned to God alone. He never worshipped anything beside God.

studies.title: My Living And My Dying
studies.meaning: Four things are named and handed over in one breath: prayer, offering, life and death. The first two are acts of worship. The second two are not acts at all, and that is what makes the list unusual. Early scholars read it as stretching devotion past what a person does, into what merely happens to them. The declaration then closes with a claim about being first, which they explain as first within this community rather than first in history.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, and this is the closing declaration of a surah that has argued at length with people who dedicated animals and crops to various powers. The instruction to say it is therefore pointed. The very practices disputed all through the surah are the ones being reassigned here. Early scholars read these verses as the surah's summing up, spoken in the first person rather than offered as one more argument.

keyTerms.note: A word for the animal offered and for acts of devotion generally. Its root also carries washing and purity, so the term joins a physical offering to the idea of being made clean.
A noun for the whole of a life rather than for the act of living. Paired with its counterpart it covers the span a person does not control, placing that under the same dedication as their prayer.

Early scholars explain first as foremost within this community rather than earliest in time, since the Quran describes earlier prophets in the same terms. It marks priority of commitment, not chronology.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Animals were dedicated by name in Arabia before Islam. A camel might be marked for a particular god, its ear slit and its milk kept back. A slaughter was announced with the name of the power it was offered to, and everyone present heard whose it was. So declaring who an offering belonged to was a public act of allegiance rather than a private intention.
studies.didYouKnow: These two verses are among the passages many Muslims say inside the prayer itself, in the opening words reported in the classical collections. So a statement that begins with the word prayer ends up being spoken during one. Early scholars note that circle when they ask how the passage came to be used.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Sincerity is defined by its reach rather than by how strongly it is felt. The list moves from what a person does to what simply happens, so what is handed over includes the parts of a life nobody chooses and nobody can perform. That makes the declaration impossible to finish by effort, and that is the point of it. It is a statement about who owns the life, not a report of something achieved. The denial of any partner then says the same thing again.

crossReferences.why: Describes sincere devotion as the whole of what was ever commanded.
Uses the same language of turning one's face over to God while doing good.
States that the flesh of offerings does not reach God, only the awareness behind them.

studies.applyIt: Before something ordinary today, say quietly who it is for. A meal, a commute, opening your laptop. Nothing long is needed, just a few words. These verses put living and dying in the same list as prayer, so the offering is meant to cover the plain hours. Those are the ones nobody thinks to dedicate.
studies.explainEasier: God tells the Prophet to say that his prayer, his worship, his life and his death all belong to God alone. God has no partner. That is what he has been told to say.

studies.title: Shall I Seek Another Lord
studies.meaning: The question comes back to one asked near the surah's beginning, and it is answered the same way. He is the Lord of everything, so there is nothing left over for anyone else to be lord of. Then come two statements about answering for what you do, and the second has become one of the most quoted lines in the Quran. No soul earns except against itself, and no bearer of burdens carries the load of another. Early scholars read the pair together. The first makes the account personal, and the second makes it impossible to pass on.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca, and the classical sources record something specific behind this. Opponents in the city made an offer. They would carry the consequences of the believers' conduct if the believers came back to the old religion. The Quran answers offers like that elsewhere in similar terms. Whether or not this verse replies to one case, the arrangement it rules out was a live proposal in a society where a clan absorbed its members' debts.

keyTerms.note: The verb for seeking something out, from a root that also produces the word for overstepping. Seeking beyond what is there and going past a limit share the same letters in Arabic.
From the root for a heavy pack, which this surah used earlier for burdens carried on the back. The verb and its object share the root, so the Arabic says a bearer does not bear a bearing.
From a root for coming after or succeeding one another, so disagreement is pictured as positions taken in turn. What is promised at the end is information about the difference, not a rebuke for it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Answering for a wrong in Arabia was shared by design. A clan paid the compensation for a killing by one of its men, and collected for injuries done to any of them. This pooling was the whole security of life without a state. A man really could take on another's debt. So an offer to carry someone's consequences was an ordinary deal rather than a flourish.
studies.didYouKnow: The statement that no bearer carries another person's burden appears five times in the Quran. It sits in five different surahs, almost always in the same words. Few sentences are repeated that steadily. The classical commentaries treat the repeating as setting out a rule rather than answering any one occasion.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two ideas that pull in opposite directions are held in one verse. God is Lord of everything, which is the largest claim there is. Each soul carries only its own load, which is the smallest unit there is. Together they rule out a universe with several authorities, and they rule out a community that can absorb one person's account. What is left is a direct relationship with nothing standing in the middle of it.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same principle and adds that a heavily laden soul finds nobody to carry any of it.
States it as one of the contents of the earlier scriptures, at the head of a short list.
Records the offer to carry another's faults and says the offer will not be honoured.

studies.applyIt: Think of a responsibility you have quietly handed to someone else: a decision you let a parent make, or a moral question you handed to an institution. Take one of them back this week and decide it yourself. This verse says the load cannot be transferred, which means the decision was never theirs to hold.
studies.explainEasier: Should I look for a lord other than God, when He is the Lord of everything. Nobody earns anything except against himself, and no one carries another person's load. In the end you all go back to your Lord.

studies.title: Successors Upon The Earth
studies.meaning: The surah closes by naming what people are. They come after others, set on the earth in their turn, and some are raised above others in degrees. The reason given for the difference is a test, and the test lies in what you were given rather than in what you were denied. Early scholars note that the unevenness itself is called the trial. Two names then close the verse. One is swift consequence, the other is forgiveness and mercy. The ending stays open at both ends.
studies.historicalContext: Mecca. This is the last verse of a surah that has been arguing for a hundred and sixty-five verses about who God is and what may be said in His name. The listeners held rank in a city built on rank. The surah's last word to them calls their arrangement a test rather than a verdict. It does not abolish the ranks, and it does not approve them either.

keyTerms.note: The plural of one who comes after another, from the root for succession. The word names people by their position in a sequence rather than by any authority, so it describes a turn rather than a title.
Steps of a stair, the third appearance of this word in the surah. It has already been used for a prophet's raising and for the grading of outcomes, and here it names ordinary social difference.
From a root meaning to wear something out by use, as a garment is tested by being worn. A trial in this vocabulary reveals what a thing is made of rather than punishing it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca ran on degrees you could see. Some families held the offices of the sanctuary. Some paid for caravans, some worked them, and some were owned. Nobody there imagined it could be otherwise, and the differences showed every day, in where you sat and how you spoke and who greeted whom first. Calling that whole structure a set of exam conditions said something the city had never heard.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for degrees turns up three times in this surah. First it describes a prophet being raised. Then it describes the grading of every person by what they did. Here it names plain social rank. One word covers being lifted by God, the outcome of a life, and a place in the world.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Unevenness is not defended here, and it is not swept away either. It is given a purpose instead, which is a harder and more useful place to stand. Whoever holds more is holding a test rather than a prize. Whoever holds less sits the same exam with a different paper. The two names at the end leave the ending unsettled on purpose. A surah about answering for what you do closes with forgiveness as its last word.

crossReferences.why: Names the same role at the beginning of the human story, one placed on the earth in succession.
States the same purpose for life and death, a test of which of you is better in conduct.
Gives a reason for the raising in degrees, so that people may make use of one another.

studies.applyIt: Take one advantage you hold that you did not earn: where you were born, an education, a body that works. Name it as an exam question rather than a possession, and ask what it is asking of you. This is the surah's last word, and it turns a fact about your life into something addressed to you.
studies.explainEasier: God put people on the earth to take their turn. He gave some more than others, and that is part of the test. What you do with what you were given is the thing being tested.
